about: Clinical Medicine is a shared UK-wide revision pack, not the syllabus of any one university. It covers the core of adult medicine that clinical students meet on the wards and in finals: history and examination, cardiology, respiratory, gastroenterology, neurology, endocrinology and diabetes, renal medicine and acute medical emergencies, aligned to the GMC's MLA content map (the version used for assessments from September 2026). Earlier-year students meeting patients for the first time (for example in Cambridge's Preparing for Patients strand) can use the history and examination topic. Guideline points are labelled with the month they were checked and should be re-checked against the current version. This is educational revision material, not clinical advice, and it gives no drug doses.

notes.h: Clinical history, examination and presenting findings
notes.overview: Most diagnoses are suggested by the history; examination and bedside tests then test that hypothesis. This topic covers the structure of a medical history, the Calgary–Cambridge consultation model, the examination routine, high-yield signs and their mechanisms, and how to present a patient concisely.
objectives: Take a structured history, including SOCRATES for pain, a drug history with the nature of any allergy, and pack-years.
Explain why discriminating questions and signs change the likelihood of a diagnosis.
Distinguish upper from lower motor neurone signs and explain the mechanism of each.
Interpret peripheral signs such as clubbing, splinter haemorrhages and koilonychia.
Present a patient with a one-line summary, discriminating positives and negatives, a differential and a plan.

sections.h: Structure of the history and consultation
sections.body:
- Presenting complaint in the patient's words, then the history of the presenting complaint. For pain use SOCRATES: site, onset, character, radiation, associated features, timing, exacerbating and relieving factors, severity.
- Past medical and surgical history, including previous similar episodes.
- Drug history and allergies: record each drug and the nature of the reaction, because a rash or anaphylaxis (allergy) is very different from nausea (intolerance).
- Family history; social history (occupation, housing, daily function, driving, alcohol in units a week, smoking in pack-years); systems review.
- Pack-years = (cigarettes a day ÷ 20) × years smoked. Example: 15 a day for 40 years = 0.75 × 40 = 30 pack-years.
- ICE: the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations.
The Calgary–Cambridge model organises the consultation into initiating the session, gathering information, physical examination, explanation and planning, and closing, with providing structure and building the relationship as continuous tasks. Start with open questions, then funnel to closed ones, and summarise back to check understanding.

- Clinical reasoning is probabilistic. The history sets a pre-test probability; a discriminating question or sign (one that is common in one diagnosis and uncommon in the alternatives) shifts that probability far more than a non-specific one.
- This is why OSCE mark schemes reward targeted questions and relevant negatives rather than an exhaustive list.
- Upper motor neurone (UMN) lesions remove descending inhibition from the spinal reflex arc, so tone and reflexes increase (spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus) and the plantar response becomes extensor; the muscle is still innervated, so there is little wasting and no fasciculation.
- Lower motor neurone (LMN) lesions cut the final pathway to muscle: tone and reflexes fall, the denervated muscle wastes and individual motor units fire spontaneously (fasciculation).
- The mechanism of finger clubbing is not fully understood (it remains contested), so treat clubbing as a marker of underlying disease rather than something you can explain with certainty.

- Clubbing: lung cancer, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, infective endocarditis, congenital (cyanotic) heart disease, inflammatory bowel disease and cirrhosis. Clubbing is not a feature of COPD itself, so clubbing in someone with COPD should prompt a search for another cause, especially lung cancer.
- Splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions (painless palmar macules) and Osler nodes (painful finger-pulp nodules) suggest infective endocarditis.
- Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) suggests iron deficiency.
- UMN pattern: increased tone, pyramidal weakness, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars. LMN pattern: wasting, fasciculation, reduced tone, reduced or absent reflexes in the distribution of the affected root or nerve.
Examination routine: clean hands, introduce yourself, confirm identity, explain and gain consent, offer a chaperone, position and expose appropriately (about 45° for cardiorespiratory examination), inspect from the end of the bed, then hands, arms, face, neck and the chest or abdomen.

sections.h: Bedside tests that complete an examination
sections.body:
Finish with the 'to complete' items: a full set of observations, capillary glucose, urine dipstick, ECG where relevant, and targeted bloods or imaging.
- Lying and standing blood pressure: NICE NG136 defines postural hypotension as a fall in systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more (or diastolic of 10 mmHg or more) on standing; measure after the person has stood for at least 1 minute. Example: lying 132/80, standing 106/74 gives a 26 mmHg systolic fall.
- Capillary glucose is quick and changes management in anyone who is confused, drowsy, fitting or has focal neurology, because hypoglycaemia can mimic all of these.
- A test is most useful when its result would change what you do; a 'positive' test in a patient with a very low pre-test probability is often a false positive.
Thresholds such as the postural drop are set by guidelines and can change; check the current version.

sections.h: Clinical application: the confused older patient
sections.body:
A 78-year-old man is brought in 'off legs' and newly confused. He cannot give a reliable history. The task is to build one from other sources:
- Collateral history from a relative or carer: baseline cognition and function, speed of onset (hours to days suggests delirium), falls, intake, recent illness.
- GP and pharmacy records for the drug history: new sedatives, anticholinergics, opioids or diuretics are common contributors.
- Then a focused examination: observations including temperature and capillary glucose, hydration, chest, abdomen (urinary retention), neurology for focal signs.
Present him as: 'A 78-year-old man with a background of hypertension presenting with two days of acute confusion and reduced mobility. Positives: temperature 38.2 °C and new crackles at the right base. Important negatives: no focal neurology, glucose normal. Most likely delirium secondary to pneumonia; differentials include urinary sepsis and medication effects. I would like a chest X-ray, bloods and cultures.' Remember to assess capacity for each decision rather than assuming its absence.

- Students often think a longer list of negatives impresses examiners. In fact only discriminating negatives help, because they rule something important in or out.
- Students often record 'allergic to penicillin' and stop. The reaction must be documented, because intolerance (nausea) does not carry the same risk as anaphylaxis and mislabelling can deny a patient the best antibiotic.
- Students often divide by 10 when calculating pack-years. A pack is 20 cigarettes, so 10 a day for 20 years is 10 pack-years, not 20.
- Students often assume clubbing in a patient with COPD is due to the COPD. COPD does not cause clubbing, so look for another cause.
- Students often treat confusion as meaning the patient lacks capacity. Capacity is decision-specific and must be assessed, not assumed.

notes.h: Cardiology: acute coronary syndromes, heart failure, atrial fibrillation and hypertension
notes.overview: Acute coronary syndromes are usually caused by plaque rupture with thrombus; the ECG decides the reperfusion pathway and troponin separates infarction from unstable angina. Heart failure, atrial fibrillation and hypertension are the commonest chronic cardiac problems, and NICE sets most of the thresholds used in UK practice.
objectives: Explain how plaque rupture and thrombus produce the spectrum of acute coronary syndromes.
Interpret ECG changes to localise an infarct and name the likely culprit artery.
Apply the NICE reperfusion criteria for STEMI.
Distinguish the roles of NT-proBNP and echocardiography in suspected heart failure.
Calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc and apply NICE step 1 hypertension treatment choices.

sections.body:
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) covers ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI) and unstable angina.
- Myocardial injury is a cardiac troponin above the 99th centile of the upper reference limit. Acute MI needs a rise and/or fall of troponin with at least one value above that limit plus evidence of ischaemia: symptoms, new ischaemic ECG changes, new Q waves, imaging evidence or thrombus at angiography (Fourth Universal Definition, 2018).
- Unstable angina has ischaemic symptoms without a troponin rise.
ECG territories (typical culprit arteries):
- II, III, aVF: inferior (usually right coronary artery), often with reciprocal depression in I and aVL.
- V1–V4: anteroseptal (left anterior descending).
- I, aVL, V5–V6: lateral (circumflex).
- Posterior: ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3; posterior leads V7–V9 show the elevation.

sections.h: From plaque to infarct, and why the heart fails
sections.body:
- A lipid-rich plaque with a thin fibrous cap ruptures or erodes, exposing thrombogenic material. Platelets adhere and aggregate and the coagulation cascade forms thrombus.
- Complete, persistent occlusion causes transmural ischaemia: ST elevation. Partial or intermittent occlusion causes subendocardial ischaemia, which is the most vulnerable layer because it is furthest from the epicardial arteries and compressed during systole: ST depression or T-wave inversion.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: falling cardiac output activates the sympathetic system and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. These support blood pressure in the short term, but cause salt and water retention, vasoconstriction and adverse remodelling. That is why drugs that block these systems improve survival, whereas diuretics only relieve congestion.
- Atrial fibrillation: chaotic atrial activity means no effective atrial contraction, so blood stagnates, especially in the left atrial appendage, and can clot and embolise to the brain.

- ACS: central, heavy chest pain at rest lasting more than about 15 minutes, often radiating to the arm or jaw, with sweating, nausea or breathlessness.
- Heart failure: exertional breathlessness, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle oedema; signs include a raised JVP, basal crackles, a third heart sound and peripheral oedema.
- Atrial fibrillation: palpitations, breathlessness or no symptoms; an irregularly irregular pulse, confirmed on a 12-lead ECG (no P waves, irregular narrow QRS complexes).
- Hypertension is usually silent and found by measurement.

- Suspected ACS: 12-lead ECG immediately and serial high-sensitivity troponin. Do not wait for troponin if the ECG shows STEMI.
- Suspected heart failure (NICE NG106): measure NT-proBNP first. Above 2,000 ng/L, refer for specialist assessment and echocardiography within 2 weeks; 400–2,000 ng/L, within 6 weeks; below 400 ng/L in an untreated person, heart failure is less likely. Obesity, African or African-Caribbean family background and treatment with heart-failure drugs lower the level; renal and other conditions can raise it.
- Echocardiography classifies heart failure by ejection fraction (reduced: 40% or less).
- Atrial fibrillation (NICE NG196): CHA₂DS₂-VASc for stroke risk (congestive heart failure 1, hypertension 1, age 75 or over 2, diabetes 1, previous stroke/TIA/thromboembolism 2, vascular disease 1, age 65–74 1, female sex 1); ORBIT for bleeding risk.
- Hypertension (NICE NG136): if clinic BP is 140/90 or higher, confirm with ambulatory or home monitoring; diagnose if the average is 135/85 or higher.

notes.h: Respiratory: asthma, COPD, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism and pneumothorax
notes.overview: Respiratory emergencies are recognised from the history, observations and a blood gas. Acute asthma is graded by objective severity features; COPD exacerbations need controlled oxygen and NIV when acidosis persists; CURB65 grades pneumonia; the Wells score steers PE testing; and pneumothorax management now depends on symptoms more than size.
objectives: Grade acute asthma using objective features and explain why a normal PaCO₂ is dangerous.
Interpret an arterial blood gas to identify type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure.
Apply CURB65 and the two-level PE Wells score.
Explain why oxygen targets differ in people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.
Outline current principles for managing pneumothorax.

sections.body:
- Respiratory failure: type 1 is PaO₂ below 8 kPa with a normal or low PaCO₂; type 2 is PaO₂ below 8 kPa with PaCO₂ above about 6.0 kPa (values approximate).
- Asthma is variable, largely reversible airway narrowing with airway inflammation. COPD is persistent airflow obstruction, mostly from smoking: post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7 (NICE NG115).
- Pneumonia is infection of the lung parenchyma with new consolidation; severity in hospital is graded with CURB65. Aspiration favours the right lower lobe (the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical).
- Pulmonary embolism (PE) is usually thrombus from the deep leg veins lodging in the pulmonary arteries.
- Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space: primary without lung disease, secondary with it (e.g. COPD).

- Type 1 failure arises mainly from ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) mismatch or shunt: alveoli that are perfused but poorly ventilated (pneumonia, oedema, PE redistributing flow). CO₂ is cleared by the remaining well-ventilated alveoli, so PaCO₂ is normal or low.
- Type 2 failure is hypoventilation: too little air moves (exhaustion, COPD, sedative drugs, neuromuscular weakness), so CO₂ rises.
- In acute asthma, a breathless patient hyperventilates and should have a low PaCO₂. A 'normal' PaCO₂ means ventilation is failing to keep up, a sign of exhaustion; a raised PaCO₂ marks near-fatal asthma.
- In some people with chronic hypercapnia, high-concentration oxygen worsens hypercapnia, mainly by releasing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (increasing V/Q mismatch) and through the Haldane effect, with loss of hypoxic drive a smaller contributor. Hence controlled oxygen.
- Large PE raises pulmonary vascular resistance, so the right ventricle fails and BP falls.

Acute asthma in adults (BTS/NICE/SIGN pathway):
- Acute severe: any one of PEF 33–50% of best or predicted, respiratory rate 25/min or more, heart rate 110/min or more, inability to complete sentences in one breath.
- Life-threatening: PEF below 33%, SpO₂ below 92%, silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, arrhythmia, hypotension, exhaustion or altered consciousness; on a blood gas, a 'normal' PaCO₂, PaO₂ below 8 kPa or a low pH.
- Near-fatal: raised PaCO₂ or need for mechanical ventilation.
CURB65 (NICE NG250): one point each for confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate 30 or more, systolic BP below 90 or diastolic 60 or less, age 65 or over. 0–1 low risk, 2 intermediate, 3–5 high. In the community CRB65 is used (no urea).

- Arterial blood gas in anyone with low saturations, suspected hypercapnia or severe asthma; chest X-ray for consolidation, pneumothorax or alternative diagnoses.

- PE: anticoagulation (apixaban or rivaroxaban first line unless exceptions such as renal impairment, active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome or haemodynamic instability); consider thrombolysis if haemodynamically unstable.
- Pneumothorax (BTS 2023): size alone is no longer an indication for intervention; conservative management can be considered if minimally symptomatic; ambulatory devices, needle aspiration or a drain otherwise.

notes.h: Gastroenterology: upper GI bleeding, chronic liver disease and inflammatory bowel disease
notes.overview: Upper GI bleeding is resuscitated first, then risk-scored (Blatchford before endoscopy, Rockall after) and endoscoped on a timetable set by stability. Cirrhosis decompensates with ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or variceal bleeding. Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease differ in distribution and depth, and acute severe colitis is a medical–surgical emergency.
objectives: Explain why portal hypertension causes varices, ascites and splenomegaly.
Apply the Blatchford score and NICE timing rules in upper GI bleeding.
Interpret liver blood tests as hepatitic or cholestatic.
Distinguish ulcerative colitis from Crohn's disease and recognise acute severe colitis.
Explain how to test correctly for coeliac disease.

sections.body:
- Upper GI bleeding presents with haematemesis or melaena (black, tarry stool from digested blood). Common causes are peptic ulcer, oesophagitis, varices and Mallory–Weiss tears.
- Chronic liver disease commonly results from alcohol, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and viral hepatitis B and C. Decompensation means ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or variceal bleeding.
- Liver blood tests: a hepatitic pattern has ALT/AST rising out of proportion to ALP (viral, drug, ischaemic, autoimmune); a cholestatic pattern is dominated by ALP and GGT (stones, malignancy, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, drugs). An AST:ALT ratio above 2 supports alcohol-related disease.
- Inflammatory bowel disease: ulcerative colitis (UC) is continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum proximally, without granulomas or fistulae; Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gut with skip lesions, transmural inflammation, granulomas, strictures and fistulae.

- Portal hypertension: fibrosis and nodules in cirrhosis raise resistance to portal flow. Blood is diverted through portosystemic collaterals at the gastro-oesophageal junction (varices), rectum and umbilicus. Splenic congestion causes splenomegaly and platelet sequestration (low platelets).
- Ascites: portal hypertension plus splanchnic vasodilatation lowers effective arterial volume, activating renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and ADH, so the kidneys retain salt and water; low albumin reduces oncotic pressure.
- Encephalopathy: the failing liver and portosystemic shunting let gut-derived toxins, especially ammonia, reach the brain. Precipitants include GI bleeding (a protein load), infection, constipation, sedatives and electrolyte disturbance.
- Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: gut bacteria translocate into ascitic fluid, which has poor defences.
- Urea rises in upper GI bleeding because blood proteins are digested and absorbed, which is why urea features in the Blatchford score.
- Transmural Crohn's inflammation explains fistulae and strictures; superficial UC inflammation explains bloody diarrhoea and the continuous pattern.

- Variceal bleeding is suggested by known cirrhosis or stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly) with a brisk haematemesis.
- Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis can be subtle: fever, abdominal pain, worsening encephalopathy or renal function in a patient with ascites; diagnosed by an ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250 cells/mm³.
- UC: bloody diarrhoea with urgency; associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis. Crohn's: abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, perianal disease and fistulae.
- Acute severe UC (Truelove and Witts): more than 6 stools a day plus systemic toxicity such as pulse above 90, fever, haemoglobin below about 105 g/L or ESR above 30 (local versions differ slightly in thresholds).
- Coeliac disease: diarrhoea, bloating, iron deficiency, weight loss, or no symptoms; associated with type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease.

- NICE CG141: use the Blatchford score at first assessment and the full Rockall score after endoscopy. Consider early discharge for patients with a pre-endoscopy Blatchford score of 0.
- Endoscopy: immediately after resuscitation for unstable patients with severe bleeding; within 24 hours of admission for all others.
- Diagnostic ascitic tap in anyone with ascites who is admitted or deteriorates: neutrophil count, culture and albumin.
- Acute severe UC: stool cultures and C. difficile toxin, inflammatory markers, an abdominal X-ray for colonic dilatation (toxic megacolon), and flexible sigmoidoscopy.
- Coeliac disease: tissue transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA (to detect IgA deficiency) while the person is still eating gluten (Coeliac UK: gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks); duodenal biopsy usually confirms, although some adults with very high antibody levels can be diagnosed without biopsy after specialist discussion.

- Upper GI bleeding: ABCDE resuscitation, large-bore access, group and crossmatch, then risk scoring and endoscopy. NICE CG141 advises against acid-suppression drugs before endoscopy for suspected non-variceal bleeding; proton pump inhibitors are given after endoscopy when stigmata of recent haemorrhage are found.
- Suspected variceal bleeding: terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation; band ligation for oesophageal varices; consider TIPS if bleeding is not controlled.
- SBP: prompt antibiotics.
- Hepatic encephalopathy: find and treat precipitants; laxative treatment (lactulose) is standard.
- Acute severe UC: admit, IV corticosteroids, VTE prophylaxis, fluids and close monitoring with joint gastroenterology and colorectal surgical care. If there is no adequate response after about 3 days, rescue medical therapy (e.g. anti-TNF) or colectomy is considered.

- SBP: prompt antibiotics.

- Students often think a raised urea in a GI bleed means kidney injury. It often reflects digestion and absorption of blood proteins.

notes.h: Neurology: stroke, TIA, subarachnoid haemorrhage, seizures and neuromuscular emergencies
notes.overview: In acute neurology, time and localisation drive decisions. notes.h: Endocrinology and diabetes: diagnosis, DKA, HHS, thyroid and adrenal disease
notes.overview: Diabetes is diagnosed with HbA1c or glucose thresholds. Its hyperglycaemic emergencies differ: DKA is insulin deficiency with ketoacidosis, HHS is profound dehydration and hyperosmolality with little ketosis. Thyroid and adrenal emergencies are less common but dangerous, and adrenal crisis must be treated before tests return.
objectives: Apply the diagnostic criteria for diabetes and recognise when HbA1c is unreliable.
Explain the pathophysiology of DKA, including why potassium falls during treatment.
Distinguish DKA from HHS and explain why their fluid and insulin priorities differ.
Recognise the electrolyte pattern and emergency management of adrenal crisis.
Outline initial drug choices for type 2 diabetes under the 2026 NICE update.

sections.body:
- Diabetes can be diagnosed with HbA1c 48 mmol/mol or more, fasting plasma glucose 7.0 mmol/L or more, random glucose 11.1 mmol/L or more with symptoms, or a 2-hour OGTT value of 11.1 mmol/L or more. Without symptoms, a diagnostic result must be confirmed by a repeat test.
- HbA1c 42–47 mmol/mol indicates non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (high risk).
- HbA1c reflects average glucose over about 2–3 months and is unsuitable for children and young people, suspected type 1 diabetes, symptoms for less than 2 months, acutely ill people, pregnancy, and conditions that change red cell lifespan or haemoglobin (haemoglobinopathies, haemolysis, recent transfusion).
- Type 1 is autoimmune beta-cell destruction; type 2 is insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell failure.

- DKA: absolute insulin deficiency with high counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines) increases hepatic glucose output and lipolysis. Free fatty acids go to the liver and are turned into ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate), causing a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis. Hyperglycaemia causes an osmotic diuresis with loss of water, sodium and potassium.
- Potassium: acidosis and insulin lack shift potassium out of cells, so serum potassium may be normal or high even though total-body potassium is depleted. Insulin drives potassium back into cells, so it falls during treatment and needs replacing.
- Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation that lowers PaCO₂.
- HHS: enough insulin is present to suppress ketogenesis, but not hyperglycaemia. It develops over days, mainly in older people with type 2 diabetes, causing severe dehydration and very high osmolality.
- Adrenal insufficiency: loss of cortisol causes hypotension and hypoglycaemia; in primary (adrenal) disease loss of aldosterone also causes salt wasting (hyponatraemia) and hyperkalaemia, and high ACTH causes pigmentation.

- DKA (JBDS 2023) requires all three: blood ketones above 3.0 mmol/L (or urine ketones 2+ or more), glucose above 11 mmol/L or known diabetes, and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3. Symptoms: thirst, polyuria, vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, Kussmaul breathing, ketotic breath.
- Markers of severe DKA needing senior review and consideration of level 2 care include ketones above 6.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L, pH below 7.0, potassium below 3.5 mmol/L on admission, GCS below 12, SpO₂ below 92% on air, systolic BP below 90 mmHg, pulse above 100 or below 60, and anion gap above 16.
- HHS: marked hypovolaemia, glucose usually above 30 mmol/L, osmolality usually above 320 mOsm/kg, without significant ketonaemia or acidosis.
- Hyperthyroidism: weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, palpitations; Graves' adds eye disease and TSH receptor antibodies.
- Adrenal crisis: hypotension or shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia; often triggered by infection, injury or surgery, or by stopping long-term steroids.

- DKA: capillary or blood ketones, venous blood gas (pH, bicarbonate, potassium), glucose, U&E, FBC, and a search for the precipitant (infection screen, ECG). Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); example: 134 − (100 + 8) = 26 mmol/L, raised.
- HHS: calculated osmolality = 2 × Na⁺ + glucose + urea (all in mmol/L). Example: 2 × 150 + 46 + 18 = 364 mOsm/kg.
- Thyroid: TSH first; low TSH with raised free T4/T3 means primary hyperthyroidism; TSH receptor antibodies support Graves' disease.
- Suspected adrenal insufficiency: a morning cortisol and a short Synacthen test (cortisol before and after synthetic ACTH); in suspected adrenal crisis take a blood sample for cortisol but never delay treatment for results.

- DKA (JBDS 2023): IV fluids to restore circulating volume; a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion; continue the person's usual long-acting basal insulin; potassium added to fluids according to level (not while above 5.5 mmol/L); add glucose when blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L so insulin can keep clearing ketones; resolution when ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH is above 7.3.
- HHS: fluids first; insulin only if there is significant ketonaemia (JBDS: above 1 mmol/L) or glucose stops falling with fluids alone; VTE prophylaxis because of high thrombotic risk.
- Type 2 diabetes (NICE NG28, 2026): for most adults, offer modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor (including those with heart failure, or CKD with eGFR above 30); with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease also offer subcutaneous semaglutide; in early-onset type 2 diabetes consider adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist or tirzepatide; in frailty, offer an SGLT2 inhibitor only if it does not put the person at risk of volume depletion or hypotension.
- Hyperthyroidism: beta-blocker for symptoms; thionamides, radioactive iodine or surgery; warn patients on thionamides to report a sore throat (agranulocytosis).
- Adrenal crisis: immediate parenteral hydrocortisone and IV fluids, then treat the trigger; patients need sick-day rules, an emergency injection kit and an NHS Steroid Emergency Card (NICE NG243).

notes.h: Renal medicine: acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia and chronic kidney disease
notes.overview: Acute kidney injury is staged by creatinine and urine output and grouped by cause into pre-renal, intrinsic and post-renal. Hyperkalaemia is the most immediately dangerous complication and is treated by protecting the heart, shifting potassium into cells and removing it. Chronic kidney disease is classified by GFR and albuminuria and is a major cardiovascular risk state.
objectives: Stage AKI using KDIGO creatinine criteria.
Distinguish pre-renal, intrinsic and post-renal AKI using history, urinalysis and imaging.
Explain the ECG changes of hyperkalaemia and why calcium is given first.
Apply the protect–shift–remove approach to hyperkalaemia.
Classify CKD by GFR and ACR and state NICE referral criteria.

sections.body:
- AKI (KDIGO creatinine criteria): stage 1 is a rise of 26.5 µmol/L or more within 48 hours, or to 1.5–1.9 times baseline within 7 days; stage 2 is 2.0–2.9 times baseline; stage 3 is 3 times baseline or more, a creatinine of 354 µmol/L or more, or starting renal replacement therapy. Oliguria (urine output below 0.5 ml/kg/hour) also defines AKI.
- Causes: pre-renal (hypovolaemia, sepsis, heart failure), intrinsic renal (acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis, rhabdomyolysis) and post-renal (obstruction).
- CKD: abnormal kidney function or structure present for more than 3 months. Classified by GFR category (G1 90 or more, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 below 15 ml/min/1.73 m²) and albumin:creatinine ratio (A1 below 3, A2 3–30, A3 above 30 mg/mmol).
- Hyperkalaemia (UK Kidney Association): mild 5.5–5.9, moderate 6.0–6.4, severe 6.5 mmol/L or more.

- Pre-renal AKI: reduced renal perfusion lowers GFR; the tubules still work, so they conserve sodium and concentrate urine (low urine sodium, high osmolality). Prolonged ischaemia damages tubular cells: acute tubular necrosis (ATN), in which the tubules can no longer conserve sodium.
- ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs and diuretics impair the kidney's ability to maintain GFR when perfusion is low (ACE inhibitors and ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole; NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation), which is why they are withheld in AKI.
- Hyperkalaemia raises the resting membrane potential of cardiac cells towards threshold, initially increasing excitability and speeding repolarisation (peaked T waves), then inactivating sodium channels so conduction slows (flattened P waves, prolonged PR, broad QRS), progressing to a sine-wave pattern and ventricular fibrillation or asystole.
- Calcium raises the threshold potential, restoring the gap between resting and threshold potential; it stabilises the myocardium but does not lower potassium.
- Insulin and beta₂ agonists stimulate the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, moving potassium into cells temporarily.

- AKI is often found on bloods; look for the cause (sepsis, drugs, a palpable bladder) and the fluid state.
- Urinalysis: blood and protein suggest glomerulonephritis (nephritic picture with red cell casts); leucocytes and nitrites suggest infection; a 'clean' dipstick fits pre-renal or ATN.
- Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema (with hyperlipidaemia and VTE risk). Nephritic syndrome: haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, oliguria and rising creatinine.
- Hyperkalaemia is usually silent until arrhythmia; weakness can occur. ECG changes: peaked T waves, flattened or absent P waves, broad QRS, bradycardia, sine wave, ventricular arrhythmia.
- Complications of advanced CKD: renal anaemia, CKD–mineral and bone disorder, acidosis, hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, hypertension and cardiovascular disease.

- Compare creatinine with a baseline; check potassium, bicarbonate (venous gas), urine dipstick before catheterisation if possible, fluid balance and a medication review.
- Renal tract ultrasound when obstruction is suspected (e.g. history of urological problems or a palpable bladder) or the cause is unclear.
- Urine sodium and osmolality can help separate pre-renal states from ATN, though diuretics confound them.
- ECG in every patient with hyperkalaemia; repeat potassium to exclude a haemolysed sample, but do not delay treatment when ECG changes are present.
- CKD: eGFR on two occasions at least 3 months apart and urine ACR; NICE NG203 refers adults to specialists for a 5-year kidney failure risk above 5% (four-variable Kidney Failure Risk Equation), ACR 70 mg/mmol or more (unless due to diabetes and already appropriately treated), ACR above 30 with haematuria, a sustained significant fall in eGFR, hypertension uncontrolled on four drugs, or suspected genetic causes.

- AKI: assess volume status and give fluids if hypovolaemic; treat sepsis; stop or withhold nephrotoxic and risky drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, diuretics; review metformin and renally cleared drugs); relieve obstruction (catheter, nephrostomy); monitor fluid balance, creatinine and potassium; restart withheld drugs when the kidneys recover.
- Indications for urgent renal replacement therapy: refractory hyperkalaemia, severe metabolic acidosis, fluid overload with pulmonary oedema unresponsive to treatment, uraemic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis) and some poisonings.
- Hyperkalaemia (UKKA, updated July 2026): protect the heart with IV calcium salts if there are ECG changes; shift potassium into cells with insulin–glucose (monitoring glucose for hypoglycaemia), with nebulised salbutamol as an adjunct in severe cases, not alone; remove potassium with a binder (e.g. sodium zirconium cyclosilicate), treat the cause and stop contributing drugs; dialysis if refractory. Routine IV sodium bicarbonate is not recommended.
- CKD: blood-pressure control; an ACE inhibitor or ARB for hypertension with ACR above 30 mg/mmol; statin for cardiovascular risk; SGLT2 inhibitors slow progression in many patients; manage anaemia and bone–mineral disease.

Mr Ahmed, 82, with hypertension and heart failure, has had 4 days of diarrhoea. He takes ramipril, furosemide, spironolactone and ibuprofen. Creatinine 245 µmol/L (baseline 98), potassium 6.3 mmol/L, BP 96/60, ECG shows peaked T waves only. 245 ÷ 98 = 2.5 times baseline: AKI stage 2, most likely pre-renal from volume loss, worsened by an ACE inhibitor, diuretics and an NSAID. His potassium is moderate (6.0–6.4) but there is an ECG change, so he receives IV calcium to protect the myocardium, then insulin–glucose to shift potassium, and a binder. All four contributing drugs are withheld and he gets cautious IV fluid. Potassium and glucose are rechecked after treatment, and the drugs are reviewed and restarted cautiously once kidney function recovers.

- Students often think IV calcium lowers potassium. It stabilises the myocardium for a short time; potassium is lowered by shifting and removal.
- Students often think salbutamol can be used alone for severe hyperkalaemia. UKKA advises it as an adjunct to insulin–glucose, not alone.
- Students often diagnose CKD from a single low eGFR. CKD requires abnormality for more than 3 months; one low value may be AKI.
- Students often forget to restart withheld drugs after AKI. ACE inhibitors and SGLT2 inhibitors protect hearts and kidneys long term, so review and restart when appropriate.
- Students often assume a normal urine output excludes AKI. Creatinine criteria can be met with a normal urine output.

notes.h: Acute medicine: ABCDE, NEWS2, sepsis, anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest and poisoning
notes.overview: The deteriorating patient is assessed with ABCDE and tracked with NEWS2, whose thresholds trigger urgent or emergency responses. Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from infection, anaphylaxis needs IM adrenaline first, cardiac arrest follows the RCUK ALS algorithm, and paracetamol overdose is managed with a treatment line or empirical acetylcysteine.
objectives: Apply the ABCDE approach, treating problems as they are found.
Calculate a NEWS2 score and state the response each threshold triggers.
Explain the Sepsis-3 definitions and how NEWS2 sets antibiotic timing in NICE NG253.
Outline first-line management of anaphylaxis and recognise refractory anaphylaxis.
Distinguish shockable from non-shockable arrest rhythms and list reversible causes.

sections.body:
- ABCDE (Resuscitation Council UK): airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure. Assess and treat in order of threat to life, treat problems as you find them, reassess after each intervention and call for help early.
- NEWS2 (Royal College of Physicians) scores respiratory rate, oxygen saturation (Scale 2 for confirmed hypercapnic respiratory failure), use of supplemental oxygen, systolic BP, pulse, consciousness (ACVPU, where new confusion scores 3) and temperature.
- RCP thresholds: aggregate 0–4 low risk (ward-based response); a single parameter scoring 3 is low–medium risk needing an urgent ward-based response; 5–6 medium risk, the key threshold for an urgent response; 7 or more high risk, an urgent or emergency response including staff with critical care skills.
- Sepsis-3 (2016): sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is sepsis needing vasopressors to keep mean arterial pressure at 65 mmHg or more with a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

- Sepsis: the immune response to infection causes widespread vasodilatation, capillary leak and microvascular thrombosis. Tissue perfusion falls, cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and lactate rises; organs fail (kidney, lung, brain, clotting).
- Anaphylaxis: IgE-mediated (or other) mast cell and basophil degranulation releases histamine and other mediators, causing vasodilatation, capillary leak (angioedema, hypotension) and bronchospasm. Adrenaline counters all three: alpha-1 vasoconstriction, beta-1 cardiac support and beta-2 bronchodilatation, and it reduces further mediator release.
- Cardiac arrest rhythms: VF and pulseless VT are chaotic or very fast electrical activity that a shock can reset (shockable); PEA and asystole are not (non-shockable), so outcome depends on CPR, adrenaline and fixing the cause.
- Paracetamol: in overdose, the normal conjugation pathways saturate and more is metabolised to a toxic metabolite (NAPQI). Glutathione detoxifies it until stores run out, after which hepatocytes are damaged. Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione.
- Opioids depress brainstem respiratory drive; naloxone is a short-acting competitive antagonist.

- Sepsis: suspected infection with signs of organ dysfunction (new confusion, hypotension, tachypnoea, low saturations, reduced urine output, raised lactate, mottled skin). Older or immunosuppressed people may be afebrile.
- Anaphylaxis: sudden airway (swelling, stridor, hoarseness), breathing (wheeze, hypoxia) and/or circulation (hypotension, collapse) problems, usually with skin or mucosal changes, after exposure to a trigger.
- Opioid toxicity: reduced consciousness, slow shallow breathing, pinpoint pupils.
- Paracetamol overdose is often asymptomatic early, while liver injury develops over days.

- Sepsis (NICE NG253, updated November 2025): in acute hospitals, risk is stratified using NEWS2. With suspected infection and NEWS2 7 or more (high risk): urgent senior assessment, venous blood gas including lactate, blood cultures and other bloods, and antibiotics within 1 hour of the first NEWS2 score. NEWS2 5–6 (moderate): clinician review and lactate within 1 hour, antibiotics within 3 hours unless raised to high risk. NEWS2 1–4 (low): antibiotics within 6 hours if indicated. A lactate above 2 mmol/L or AKI means the person is managed as high risk.
- Anaphylaxis: mast cell tryptase, ideally within 2 hours of onset and no later than 4 hours, with a later baseline sample; do not delay treatment.
- Paracetamol: measure the plasma level at 4 hours or later after a single acute ingestion and plot it on the single treatment line (100 mg/L at 4 hours); also LFTs, INR, U&E and venous gas.
- Cardiac arrest: blood gas and potassium help find reversible causes.

- Sepsis: antibiotics within the NICE time frame, IV fluid for hypotension or raised lactate, oxygen to target, source control (drain pus, remove infected lines), escalation to critical care for shock.
- Anaphylaxis (RCUK 2021): call for help, IM adrenaline into the anterolateral middle third of the thigh, repeat after 5 minutes if there is no improvement; high-flow oxygen and an IV fluid bolus for shock. Refractory anaphylaxis (persisting respiratory or cardiovascular problems despite two appropriate IM doses) needs an adrenaline infusion with expert help. Antihistamines are not part of initial emergency treatment and routine corticosteroids are not advised; refer to an allergy clinic.
- Adult ALS (RCUK 2025): high-quality CPR with minimal interruptions. Shockable rhythm: shock, resume CPR for 2 minutes; adrenaline and amiodarone after the third shock, then adrenaline every 3–5 minutes. Non-shockable: adrenaline as soon as possible, then every 3–5 minutes. Treat reversible causes: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and other metabolic causes, hypo/hyperthermia; thrombosis, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins.
- Paracetamol: acetylcysteine if the level is on or above the treatment line (regardless of risk factors); for staggered overdoses or when the time of ingestion is uncertain, start acetylcysteine without delay and do not use the nomogram.
- Opioid toxicity: support breathing and give naloxone, repeated as needed.

Mrs Clarke, 67, is two days after an anterior resection. She is newly confused; RR 28, SpO₂ 91% on air, BP 84/46, HR 126, temperature 38.9 °C; lactate 4.6 mmol/L and her abdomen is distended and tender.
NEWS2: RR 25 or more (3) + SpO₂ 91% on Scale 1 (3) + air (0) + systolic 84 (3) + pulse 126 (2) + new confusion (3) + temperature 38.9 (1) = 15, a high-risk emergency response.
She has suspected sepsis with hypotension and a lactate well above 2 mmol/L. ABCDE: oxygen, cultures, lactate, antibiotics within 1 hour, fluid bolus with reassessment, urine output monitoring, urgent senior and critical care review. The likely source is an anastomotic leak, so CT and source control (return to theatre) are as important as antibiotics.

- Students often give an antihistamine before adrenaline in anaphylaxis. IM adrenaline comes first; antihistamines are not part of initial emergency treatment.
- Students often think a normal temperature excludes sepsis. Older or immunosuppressed patients may be afebrile or hypothermic.
- Students often plot a staggered paracetamol overdose on the nomogram. It is only valid for a single ingestion at a known time; staggered overdoses are treated without it.
- Students often wait for a NEWS2 of 7 before escalating. A single parameter scoring 3 already needs an urgent ward-based response.

cards.f: SOCRATES in a pain history
cards.b: Site, onset, character, radiation, associated features, timing, exacerbating/relieving factors, severity.
cards.ex: A structured pain history makes it easier to separate, for example, cardiac from pleuritic chest pain.

cards.f: A patient smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 20 years. Pack-years?
cards.ex: Pack-years = packs a day × years; one pack is 20 cigarettes.

cards.f: Why must the nature of a drug reaction be recorded?
cards.b: Because true allergy (rash, angioedema, anaphylaxis) and intolerance (nausea, diarrhoea) carry different risks; recording only 'allergy' can deny a patient a needed drug or expose them to a dangerous one.
cards.ex: Write the drug, the reaction, and when it happened.

cards.f: Why does an upper motor neurone lesion cause hyperreflexia?
cards.b: Descending pathways normally inhibit the spinal stretch reflex. When they are damaged, the reflex arc is disinhibited, so tone and reflexes increase and clonus may appear.
cards.ex: The reflex arc itself (LMN) is intact in a UMN lesion.

cards.f: Why do lower motor neurone lesions cause wasting and fasciculation?
cards.b: Denervated muscle loses trophic support and wastes; spontaneous firing of surviving or damaged motor units produces visible fasciculations.
cards.ex: Fasciculation is a LMN sign; it does not occur in pure UMN lesions.

cards.f: UMN versus LMN weakness: tone, reflexes, plantars
cards.b: UMN: increased tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars, little wasting. LMN: reduced tone, reduced/absent reflexes, flexor or absent plantar response, wasting and fasciculation.
cards.ex: Mixed UMN and LMN signs together should make you think of motor neurone disease.

cards.f: A man with COPD has new finger clubbing. What does it suggest?
cards.b: Another disease, most importantly lung cancer (or bronchiectasis or fibrosis), because COPD itself does not cause clubbing. He needs a chest X-ray.
cards.ex: Clubbing is a marker of underlying disease, not a feature of COPD.

cards.f: Splinter haemorrhages, painful finger-pulp nodules and a new murmur
cards.b: Infective endocarditis (Osler nodes are painful; Janeway lesions are painless palmar macules). Take blood cultures before antibiotics.
cards.ex: Peripheral stigmata support but do not make the diagnosis; blood cultures and echocardiography do.

cards.f: Postural hypotension threshold (NICE NG136)
cards.b: A fall in systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more, or diastolic of 10 mmHg or more, on standing.
cards.ex: Guideline threshold: check the current NICE version.

cards.f: A newly confused 80-year-old cannot give a history. First two sources?
cards.b: A collateral history from family or carers (baseline, onset, function) and the GP or pharmacy drug record.
cards.ex: Delirium is defined partly by a change from baseline, which only someone who knows the patient can describe.

cards.f: Open versus closed questions: when to use each
cards.b: Open questions first, to hear the patient's story and agenda; closed questions later, to clarify specific features and discriminating details.
cards.ex: Starting closed risks missing the patient's main concern.

cards.f: Why does a discriminating sign matter more than a common one?
cards.b: A sign that is frequent in one diagnosis but rare in its alternatives shifts the probability a lot; a sign common to all options barely changes it.
cards.ex: This is the reasoning behind 'relevant negatives' in a presentation.

cards.f: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with ST depression in I and aVL
cards.b: Inferior STEMI, usually right coronary artery occlusion, with reciprocal lateral changes.
cards.ex: Reciprocal depression supports a true STEMI rather than pericarditis.

cards.f: Troponin definition of acute MI (2018)
cards.b: A rise and/or fall of cardiac troponin with at least one value above the 99th centile upper reference limit, plus evidence of acute ischaemia.
cards.ex: A raised troponin alone is myocardial injury, not necessarily MI.

cards.f: Why is the subendocardium most vulnerable to ischaemia?
cards.b: It is furthest from the epicardial coronary arteries and is compressed during systole, so its perfusion depends on diastole and falls first when supply is limited.
cards.ex: Subendocardial ischaemia produces ST depression rather than elevation.

cards.f: Why does blocking the RAAS improve survival in HFrEF but diuretics do not?
cards.b: RAAS and sympathetic activation drive salt retention, vasoconstriction and adverse remodelling; blocking them slows progression. Diuretics only remove excess fluid.
cards.ex: Diuretics treat symptoms of congestion; the four drug classes change prognosis.

cards.f: How does atrial fibrillation cause stroke?
cards.b: Loss of coordinated atrial contraction lets blood stagnate, especially in the left atrial appendage; thrombus forms and can embolise to the brain.
cards.ex: This is why AF stroke prevention uses anticoagulants, not antiplatelets alone.

cards.f: NT-proBNP 2,600 ng/L in suspected heart failure: next step (NICE NG106)?
cards.b: Refer urgently for specialist assessment and echocardiography within 2 weeks.
cards.ex: Above 2,000 ng/L: within 2 weeks; 400–2,000 ng/L: within 6 weeks.

cards.f: Score CHA₂DS₂-VASc: 72-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes
cards.b: Age 65–74 (1) + female (1) + hypertension (1) + diabetes (1) = 4, so anticoagulation is indicated.
cards.ex: Age 75 or over scores 2; previous stroke/TIA scores 2.

cards.f: Unstable angina versus NSTEMI
cards.b: Both are ischaemic symptoms without persistent ST elevation; NSTEMI has a troponin rise and fall above the 99th centile, unstable angina does not.
cards.ex: The ECG may look the same in both; troponin separates them.

cards.f: First-line antihypertensive for a 60-year-old white man without diabetes (NICE NG136)
cards.b: A calcium-channel blocker, because he is 55 or over and does not have type 2 diabetes.
cards.ex: ACE inhibitor/ARB if type 2 diabetes, or if under 55 and not of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin.

cards.f: NICE STEMI reperfusion rule
cards.b: Primary PCI if presenting within 12 hours of onset and PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could be given; otherwise fibrinolysis.
cards.ex: Guideline criterion (NG185); check for updates.

cards.f: ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3 and chest pain
cards.b: Possible posterior MI; record posterior leads V7–V9, which would show ST elevation.
cards.ex: The anterior leads see the posterior wall 'in reverse'.

cards.f: Resistant hypertension step 4: potassium 4.3 vs 4.9 mmol/L
cards.b: Potassium 4.5 or less: consider spironolactone. Above 4.5: consider an alpha- or beta-blocker instead.
cards.ex: Spironolactone retains potassium, so a higher baseline potassium favours an alternative.

cards.f: Why is a normal PaCO₂ dangerous in acute asthma?
cards.b: A breathless asthmatic should hyperventilate and have a low PaCO₂; a normal value means ventilation is failing because she is tiring.
cards.ex: Normal PaCO₂ is a life-threatening feature; a raised PaCO₂ means near-fatal asthma.

cards.f: Type 1 versus type 2 respiratory failure
cards.b: Both have PaO₂ below 8 kPa. Type 1: PaCO₂ normal or low (V/Q mismatch). Type 2: PaCO₂ raised (hypoventilation).
cards.ex: Look at PaCO₂ to tell them apart.

cards.f: CURB65 components
cards.b: Confusion; urea above 7 mmol/L; respiratory rate 30 or more; systolic BP below 90 or diastolic 60 or less; age 65 or over.
cards.ex: 0–1 low, 2 intermediate, 3–5 high risk (NICE NG250).

cards.f: Score CURB65: 76-year-old, alert, urea 6.2, RR 32, BP 104/58
cards.b: Age 1 + RR 1 + BP 1 (diastolic 60 or less) = 3: high risk.
cards.ex: Urea 6.2 does not score; diastolic 58 does.

cards.f: Why can high-flow oxygen worsen hypercapnia in some COPD patients?
cards.b: It releases hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (worsening V/Q mismatch) and, via the Haldane effect, reduces haemoglobin's CO₂ carriage; reduced hypoxic drive plays a smaller part.
cards.ex: So target 88–92% in those at risk, not withhold oxygen.

cards.f: ABG on air: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 8.1 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 29
cards.b: Acidaemia with raised PaCO₂ and raised bicarbonate: acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (type 2 respiratory failure if PaO₂ below 8).
cards.ex: Raised bicarbonate implies renal compensation over days, so a chronic component.

cards.f: PE Wells score 5 with CTPA available in 2 hours: next step?
cards.b: PE likely: arrange CTPA, giving interim anticoagulation if it cannot be done immediately (NICE NG158).
cards.ex: D-dimer is for the 'PE unlikely' group (4 or fewer points).

cards.f: NIV criteria in a COPD exacerbation
cards.b: pH below 7.35 and PaCO₂ above 6.5 kPa that persist or develop despite optimal medical therapy.
cards.ex: BTS/ICS guidance; give controlled oxygen and bronchodilators first.

cards.f: Acute severe versus life-threatening asthma by PEF and SpO₂
cards.b: Acute severe: PEF 33–50%. Life-threatening: PEF below 33% or SpO₂ below 92% (or other life-threatening features).
cards.ex: Any single life-threatening feature is enough.

cards.f: Why does a large PE cause hypotension?
cards.b: Obstruction raises pulmonary vascular resistance, the right ventricle dilates and fails, and left ventricular filling and cardiac output fall.
cards.ex: Haemodynamic instability is when thrombolysis is considered.

cards.f: Minimally symptomatic 22-year-old with a large primary pneumothorax: does size force a drain?
cards.b: No. BTS 2023: size alone is no longer an indication for intervention; conservative management can be considered if minimally symptomatic, with follow-up.
cards.ex: Symptoms, physiology and patient priorities guide management.

cards.f: When to use Blatchford and when Rockall (NICE CG141)
cards.b: Blatchford at first assessment (before endoscopy); full Rockall after endoscopy.
cards.ex: Blatchford 0: early discharge may be considered.

cards.f: Unstable patient with severe upper GI bleed: when is endoscopy done?
cards.b: Immediately after resuscitation; other patients within 24 hours of admission (NICE CG141).
cards.ex: Resuscitation always comes before endoscopy.

cards.f: Why does urea rise in upper GI bleeding?
cards.b: Blood in the gut is digested and its protein absorbed, raising urea; hypovolaemia adds a pre-renal component.
cards.ex: This is why urea is part of the Blatchford score.

cards.f: Why do patients with cirrhosis have low platelets?
cards.b: Portal hypertension congests the spleen, which enlarges and sequesters platelets (hypersplenism); reduced thrombopoietin production also contributes.
cards.ex: Thrombocytopenia is a clue to portal hypertension.

cards.f: How does portal hypertension cause varices?
cards.b: Raised resistance to portal flow diverts blood through portosystemic collaterals, which dilate at the gastro-oesophageal junction and can rupture.
cards.ex: Other collateral sites: rectum and umbilicus (caput medusae).

cards.f: Ascitic neutrophil count 410 cells/mm³ in a febrile patient with cirrhosis
cards.b: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (at least 250 cells/mm³ without a surgical source): start antibiotics promptly.
cards.ex: SBP can present with encephalopathy or worsening renal function rather than pain.

cards.f: ALT 820, ALP 140 (both U/L)
cards.b: Hepatitic pattern: transaminases out of proportion to ALP (viral, drug, ischaemic, autoimmune).
cards.ex: A cholestatic pattern is ALP and GGT dominant.

cards.f: Ulcerative colitis versus Crohn's disease
cards.b: UC: continuous from rectum, mucosal, no granulomas or fistulae. Crohn's: anywhere mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural, granulomas, fistulae and strictures.
cards.ex: Transmural inflammation explains fistulae in Crohn's.

cards.f: Why test for coeliac disease while the patient is still eating gluten?
cards.b: Antibodies and villous atrophy depend on gluten exposure; after a gluten-free diet both can return to normal, giving false negatives.
cards.ex: Coeliac UK: gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks before testing.

cards.f: Known cirrhosis, haematemesis, BP 88/52: which drugs at presentation?
cards.b: Terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics, alongside resuscitation, then endoscopy and band ligation (NICE CG141).
cards.ex: Treat as variceal until proven otherwise.

cards.f: UC flare: 9 bloody stools a day, pulse 104, temperature 38.1 °C
cards.b: Acute severe ulcerative colitis (Truelove and Witts): admit for IV steroids, stool cultures with C. difficile testing, abdominal X-ray and joint surgical review.
cards.ex: One systemic feature with more than 6 stools a day is enough.

cards.f: Bamford: criteria for a TACS
cards.b: All three: unilateral weakness/sensory loss of at least two of face, arm and leg; homonymous hemianopia; higher cerebral dysfunction (e.g. dysphasia, neglect).
cards.ex: Two of three (or higher dysfunction alone) = PACS.

cards.f: Right arm and face weakness, expressive dysphasia, right homonymous hemianopia
cards.b: Left TACS: all three criteria are met.
cards.ex: Dysphasia with right-sided weakness localises to the dominant (usually left) hemisphere.

cards.f: Why do lacunar strokes cause 'pure' syndromes?
cards.b: They affect small deep penetrating arteries supplying compact pathways (e.g. internal capsule), sparing the cortex, so there is no dysphasia, neglect or field loss.
cards.ex: Cortical signs exclude a lacunar stroke.

cards.f: What is the ischaemic penumbra?
cards.b: Underperfused but still viable brain around the infarct core; reperfusion aims to save it before it dies, which is why time windows matter.
cards.ex: Advanced imaging can show salvageable penumbra up to 24 hours in selected patients.

cards.f: Why wait 12 hours before LP for suspected SAH?
cards.b: Red cells in CSF need several hours to break down into bilirubin; xanthochromia then distinguishes SAH from a traumatic tap.
cards.ex: NICE NG228: at least 12 hours after onset.

cards.f: NICE NG128 approach to suspected TIA
cards.b: Aspirin straight away unless contraindicated, specialist assessment within 24 hours; do not use ABCD2 or other scores to triage.
cards.ex: Guidance changed in 2019: scores are no longer used.

cards.f: Stroke onset 'last seen well 23:00', found at 07:00 with an anterior large-vessel occlusion: options?
cards.b: Outside the 4.5-hour thrombolysis window, but thrombectomy can be offered up to 24 hours if imaging shows salvageable brain.
cards.ex: Onset time = last known well.

cards.f: Seizing for 7 minutes, IV access available: first drug class?
cards.b: A benzodiazepine (IV in hospital with resuscitation facilities); repeat once after 5–10 minutes if it continues, then a second-line agent.
cards.ex: Also check glucose and look for causes.

cards.f: Why monitor FVC, not peak flow, in Guillain–Barré syndrome?
cards.b: Facial and bulbar weakness prevent a tight seal and a forceful blast, so peak flow underestimates function unreliably; FVC tracks respiratory muscle strength.
cards.ex: Falling FVC prompts early critical care referral.

cards.f: Guillain–Barré syndrome versus spinal cord compression
cards.b: GBS: ascending weakness, areflexia, no sensory level, sphincters usually spared early. Cord compression: sensory level, UMN signs below the lesion (may be flaccid acutely), early sphincter disturbance.
cards.ex: A sensory level points to the cord.

cards.f: CSF: protein raised, white cells normal, after a diarrhoeal illness and leg weakness
cards.b: Albuminocytological dissociation, typical of Guillain–Barré syndrome.
cards.ex: CSF may be normal in the first week.

cards.f: Diagnostic HbA1c for diabetes
cards.b: 48 mmol/mol or more (repeat to confirm if asymptomatic); 42–47 mmol/mol = non-diabetic hyperglycaemia.
cards.ex: HbA1c is unreliable in children, suspected type 1, pregnancy and altered red cell turnover.

cards.f: Why is HbA1c unreliable after a recent blood transfusion or in haemolysis?
cards.b: HbA1c depends on how long red cells are exposed to glucose; transfused or short-lived red cells give a falsely low value.
cards.ex: Use glucose-based tests instead.

cards.f: How does insulin deficiency cause ketoacidosis?
cards.b: With little insulin and high glucagon, lipolysis releases fatty acids that the liver converts to ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate), producing a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis.
cards.ex: Even small amounts of insulin suppress ketogenesis, which is why HHS has little ketosis.

cards.f: Why does potassium fall during DKA treatment?
cards.b: Insulin drives potassium into cells, and fluids dilute it, unmasking total-body potassium depletion caused by osmotic diuresis and vomiting.
cards.ex: Check potassium often and replace it once it is 5.5 mmol/L or lower and urine is passed.

cards.f: JBDS 2023 diagnostic criteria for DKA
cards.b: Ketones above 3.0 mmol/L (or urine 2+), glucose above 11 mmol/L or known diabetes, and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3.
cards.ex: All three are required.

cards.f: Glucose 46, Na 150, urea 18 (mmol/L): calculated osmolality?
cards.b: 2 × 150 + 46 + 18 = 364 mOsm/kg, consistent with HHS if ketones are low.
cards.ex: Osmolality = 2Na + glucose + urea.

cards.f: DKA versus HHS
cards.b: DKA: ketones above 3, acidosis, often younger with type 1, hours to develop. HHS: very high glucose and osmolality, severe dehydration, little ketosis, older people with type 2, develops over days.
cards.ex: Mixed pictures occur.

cards.f: DKA: glucose now 12 mmol/L but ketones 2.4 and pH 7.25. What changes?
cards.b: Add IV glucose and continue the fixed-rate insulin infusion until ketones are below 0.6 and pH above 7.3.
cards.ex: The target is ketone clearance, not glucose.

cards.f: Hypotension, Na 126, K 5.9, glucose 3.2 in a patient who stopped long-term prednisolone
cards.b: Adrenal crisis: give parenteral hydrocortisone and IV fluids immediately, taking a cortisol sample without delaying treatment.
cards.ex: Stopping long-term steroids suppresses the adrenal axis.

cards.f: Why does primary adrenal failure cause hyperkalaemia and pigmentation?
cards.b: Loss of aldosterone impairs potassium excretion and sodium retention; low cortisol removes negative feedback, so ACTH (and related peptides) rises and stimulates melanocytes.
cards.ex: Secondary (pituitary) failure lacks pigmentation and usually spares aldosterone.

cards.f: Patient on carbimazole develops a sore throat and fever
cards.b: Stop the drug and check an urgent full blood count for agranulocytosis.
cards.ex: Patients must be warned about this at the start of treatment.

cards.f: Newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, no comorbidity: initial drugs (NICE NG28, 2026)?
cards.b: Modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor; SGLT2 inhibitor alone if metformin is contraindicated or not tolerated.
cards.ex: Add semaglutide if established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

cards.f: KDIGO stage 1 AKI (creatinine)
cards.b: Rise of 26.5 µmol/L or more within 48 hours, or to 1.5–1.9 × baseline within 7 days (or urine output below 0.5 ml/kg/h for 6–12 h).
cards.ex: Stage 2: 2.0–2.9 ×; stage 3: 3 × or more, 354 µmol/L or more, or RRT.

cards.f: Baseline creatinine 80, now 210 µmol/L after 3 days of diarrhoea: stage?
cards.b: 210 ÷ 80 ≈ 2.6 × baseline: AKI stage 2, likely pre-renal.
cards.ex: Always compare with a baseline.

cards.f: Why are ACE inhibitors withheld in AKI?
cards.b: They dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering glomerular pressure; when renal perfusion is already low, this further reduces GFR.
cards.ex: NSAIDs do the same at the afferent side by blocking prostaglandin-mediated dilatation.

cards.f: Why does hyperkalaemia broaden the QRS?
cards.b: Raised extracellular potassium depolarises the resting membrane and inactivates sodium channels, slowing conduction through the myocardium.
cards.ex: Earlier changes: peaked T waves; late: sine wave, VF or asystole.

cards.f: Why give IV calcium if it does not lower potassium?
cards.b: It raises the threshold potential, restoring the margin between resting and threshold potential, so it protects against arrhythmia while other treatments act.
cards.ex: Give it when there are ECG changes.

cards.f: Potassium 6.2 mmol/L with a normal ECG: which UKKA band?
cards.b: Moderate (6.0–6.4). Mild is 5.5–5.9 and severe 6.5 mmol/L or more.
cards.ex: ECG changes make any level an emergency regardless of band.

cards.f: K⁺ 7.0 mmol/L with broad QRS: order of treatment
cards.b: IV calcium first (protect), then insulin–glucose ± nebulised salbutamol (shift), then a potassium binder, treat the cause, dialysis if refractory (remove).
cards.ex: Monitor glucose after insulin and recheck potassium for rebound.

cards.f: Pre-renal AKI versus acute tubular necrosis: urine
cards.b: Pre-renal: low urine sodium, concentrated urine (tubules conserving). ATN: higher urine sodium, urine osmolality close to plasma (tubules damaged).
cards.ex: Diuretics invalidate urine sodium.

cards.f: Nephrotic versus nephritic syndrome
cards.b: Nephrotic: heavy proteinuria, low albumin, oedema, hyperlipidaemia. Nephritic: haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, oliguria, rising creatinine.
cards.ex: Dipstick blood + protein in AKI suggests glomerulonephritis: urgent renal referral.

cards.f: eGFR 38 and ACR 45 mg/mmol, stable for 6 months
cards.b: CKD G3b A3.
cards.ex: Two parameters: GFR category and albuminuria category.

cards.f: CKD with a 5-year kidney failure risk (KFRE) of 8%: refer?
cards.b: Yes. NICE NG203 refers adults with a 5-year risk above 5%, or ACR 70 mg/mmol or more (unless due to diabetes and already treated).
cards.ex: Other triggers: ACR above 30 with haematuria, sustained eGFR fall, BP uncontrolled on four drugs.

cards.f: Aggregate NEWS2 of 6 on a surgical ward: what response does the RCP chart require?
cards.b: Medium risk, the key threshold for an urgent response by a clinician or team skilled in acute illness (7 or more would need an urgent or emergency response with critical care skills).
cards.ex: A single parameter scoring 3 also needs an urgent ward-based response.

cards.f: Calculate NEWS2: RR 26, SpO₂ 93% on air, systolic 98, pulse 115, alert, 38.6 °C
cards.b: RR 3 + SpO₂ 2 + air 0 + BP 2 + pulse 2 + alert 0 + temp 1 = 10: emergency response.
cards.ex: SpO₂ 92–93% scores 2 on Scale 1; systolic 91–100 scores 2.

cards.f: Sepsis-3 definition of septic shock
cards.b: Sepsis needing vasopressors to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or more with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
cards.ex: Sepsis itself = life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection.

cards.f: Why does lactate rise in sepsis?
cards.b: Vasodilatation, capillary leak and microvascular thrombosis reduce tissue oxygen delivery, so cells use anaerobic metabolism; impaired clearance and adrenergic stimulation also contribute.
cards.ex: NICE NG253 treats lactate above 2 mmol/L as high risk.

cards.f: Suspected infection, NEWS2 8 in the emergency department: antibiotic timing (NICE NG253)?
cards.b: High risk: antibiotics within 1 hour of the first NEWS2 score, with senior review, lactate and cultures.
cards.ex: NEWS2 5–6: within 3 hours; 1–4: within 6 hours (if indicated).

cards.f: Why is adrenaline, not an antihistamine, first-line in anaphylaxis?
cards.b: Adrenaline reverses vasodilatation (alpha-1), supports the heart (beta-1), bronchodilates (beta-2) and reduces mediator release; antihistamines are slow and do not treat airway or circulatory compromise.
cards.ex: IM into the anterolateral thigh; repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement.

cards.f: Still wheezy and hypotensive after two IM adrenaline doses for anaphylaxis: next step?
cards.b: This is refractory anaphylaxis (RCUK 2021): get expert help for an adrenaline infusion, continue IV fluids and high-flow oxygen.
cards.ex: Antihistamines and steroids are not the answer to persisting airway or circulatory problems.

cards.f: Shockable versus non-shockable arrest rhythms
cards.b: Shockable: VF and pulseless VT (defibrillate). Non-shockable: PEA and asystole (CPR, adrenaline as soon as possible, treat reversible causes).
cards.ex: Adrenaline and amiodarone are given after the third shock in shockable rhythms.

cards.f: Reversible causes of cardiac arrest
cards.b: Hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and metabolic, hypo/hyperthermia; thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary), tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins.
cards.ex: The 4 Hs and 4 Ts.

cards.f: Why can't the nomogram be used for a staggered paracetamol overdose?
cards.b: The treatment line assumes a single ingestion at a known time; with several ingestions the level cannot be interpreted against time, so acetylcysteine is started without the nomogram.
cards.ex: Also start without delay if the ingestion time is uncertain.

cards.f: Why may naloxone need repeating in opioid toxicity?
cards.b: Its duration of action is shorter than that of many opioids, so respiratory depression can return as it wears off.
cards.ex: Observe and repeat or use an infusion as needed.

questions.q: Which examination finding is most typical of a lower motor neurone lesion?
questions.why: Fasciculation and wasting occur when the motor neurone or its axon is damaged, because the muscle loses its nerve supply and surviving units fire spontaneously. Clonus, an upgoing plantar and spasticity all reflect loss of descending inhibition in an upper motor neurone lesion.
optWhy: Clonus reflects disinhibited stretch reflexes, an upper motor neurone sign.
An extensor plantar response (Babinski sign) indicates corticospinal (upper motor neurone) damage.
Correct: denervated muscle wastes and shows fasciculation, the hallmark of a lower motor neurone lesion.
Spasticity (velocity-dependent increase in tone) is an upper motor neurone sign.
questions.clue: 'Most typical of a lower motor neurone lesion'.
questions.concept: Upper versus lower motor neurone signs.

followUp.q: Which finding points to an upper motor neurone lesion?
options: Brisk knee reflexes with an upgoing plantar
Wasting of the small hand muscles
followUp.why: Hyperreflexia with an extensor plantar response reflects loss of descending inhibition, an upper motor neurone pattern. Absent reflexes, fasciculation and wasting are lower motor neurone signs.

questions.q: A 62-year-old smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 25 years, then cut down to 10 a day for a further 10 years before stopping. What is his smoking history in pack-years?
questions.why: Pack-years = (cigarettes a day ÷ 20) × years for each period, then add them. First period: (20 ÷ 20) × 25 = 25. Second: (10 ÷ 20) × 10 = 5. Total 30 pack-years.
optWhy: 25 counts only the first period and ignores the later 10 years.
Correct: 25 + 5 = 30 pack-years.
35 treats all 35 years as one pack a day, ignoring that he halved his intake.
60 uses 10 cigarettes as one pack (50 + 10) instead of 20.
600 multiplies cigarettes by years (500 + 100) without dividing by 20.
questions.clue: Two periods at different rates: 20 a day for 25 years, then 10 a day for 10 years.

followUp.q: A woman smoked 15 cigarettes a day for 40 years. What is her pack-year history?
followUp.why: (15 ÷ 20) × 40 = 0.75 × 40 = 30 pack-years. 600 forgets to divide by 20; 40 counts years only; 15 counts cigarettes a day only.

questions.q: A 71-year-old man with known COPD attends for review. You notice new finger clubbing that was not recorded a year ago. He has lost some weight. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Record it as part of his COPD and review in a year
Check thyroid function for thyroid acropachy
Arrange a chest X-ray to look for an alternative cause such as lung cancer
Start a course of antibiotics for presumed infection
questions.why: COPD does not itself cause clubbing, so new clubbing in a smoker with COPD, especially with weight loss, should prompt a search for another cause, most importantly lung cancer. A chest X-ray is the appropriate first investigation.
optWhy: COPD does not cause clubbing, so attributing it to COPD risks missing lung cancer.
Thyroid acropachy is a rare cause of clubbing in Graves' disease; it is not the priority in an older smoker with weight loss.
Correct: new clubbing plus weight loss in a smoker needs a chest X-ray to look for lung cancer, bronchiectasis or fibrosis.
There are no features of acute infection; antibiotics do not address the cause of clubbing.
Nail-bed biopsy has no role in investigating clubbing.
questions.clue: New clubbing in a smoker with COPD, plus weight loss.
questions.concept: Clubbing is not caused by COPD; it is a marker of other disease.

followUp.q: A 24-year-old who injects drugs has fever, a new pansystolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages and painful nodules on the finger pulps. What is the most important first investigation?
options: Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
followUp.why: The picture suggests infective endocarditis (Osler nodes are painful finger-pulp nodules). Blood cultures taken before antibiotics are central to diagnosis and to choosing treatment; echocardiography follows.

questions.q: An 84-year-old woman is admitted from home with two days of fluctuating confusion. She cannot recall her medicines or how long she has been unwell. What is the most useful next step in building her history?
options: Wait until she is less confused before taking any history
Ask her a list of closed questions from the systems review
Document that she lacks capacity for all decisions
Perform a CT head before any further history
Obtain a collateral history from her daughter and check her GP and pharmacy medication records
questions.why: When the patient cannot give a reliable history, a collateral history establishes her baseline, how quickly the change happened (acute onset and fluctuation suggest delirium) and recent events, and the GP or pharmacy record gives an accurate drug history, since medicines commonly contribute to delirium.
optWhy: Delaying the history delays finding a treatable cause of delirium.
Closed questions to a confused patient give unreliable answers and miss the baseline.
Capacity is decision-specific and must be assessed for each decision, not assumed absent.
Imaging may be needed later, but the history decides who needs it; it is not the next step in building the history.
Correct: collateral history plus medication records give the baseline, time course and drug history.
questions.clue: Fluctuating confusion and an unreliable history.
questions.concept: Collateral history in the confused patient.

followUp.q: A patient tells you he is 'allergic to amoxicillin'. Which entry is most useful in the notes?
options: Amoxicillin: widespread itchy rash and lip swelling within an hour, aged 30
followUp.why: Recording the drug, the reaction and its timing lets later prescribers judge whether this was a true allergy (here, likely, given urticaria and angioedema) or an intolerance.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man is newly confused on the ward. Give four elements of the history you would obtain, and from whom.
markScheme: Collateral history from a relative or carer: baseline cognition and function, and the time course of the change
Drug history from the drug chart, GP record or pharmacy: new or changed medicines (e.g. sedatives, opioids, anticholinergics)
Symptoms of precipitants: infection (cough, urinary symptoms, fever), pain, constipation, urinary retention, falls or head injury
Alcohol intake (withdrawal) and recent intake of food and fluid, from the patient, family and nursing staff
Nursing observations and notes: when the change started, sleep, behaviour, fluid balance
questions.modelAnswer: I would ask the patient what I can, but rely heavily on others. From his family or carer I would obtain a collateral history of his usual cognition and function and when and how quickly the change began, because an acute, fluctuating change suggests delirium. From the drug chart, GP record and pharmacy I would establish his medicines and any recent changes, especially sedatives, opioids and anticholinergic drugs. From the nursing staff and notes I would learn when the confusion started, his observations, sleep, oral intake, bowel and bladder function. I would ask about symptoms of precipitants such as infection, pain, constipation, urinary retention or a fall, and about alcohol intake because withdrawal can present this way.
questions.concept: Building a history from collateral sources in delirium.

questions.q: Which feature is required, in addition to a rise and/or fall of troponin above the 99th centile, to diagnose an acute myocardial infarction?
options: A troponin at least five times the upper reference limit
questions.why: The Fourth Universal Definition requires a dynamic troponin above the 99th centile plus evidence of ischaemia (symptoms, new ischaemic ECG changes, new Q waves, imaging or thrombus). Without ischaemia, a raised troponin indicates myocardial injury, which has many causes.
optWhy: No fixed multiple of the upper limit is required for a type 1 MI.
ST elevation defines STEMI, but NSTEMI is also an MI without ST elevation.
Correct: troponin plus evidence of acute ischaemia defines acute MI.
Ejection fraction classifies heart failure and is not part of the MI definition.
questions.clue: 'In addition to a rise and/or fall of troponin'.

followUp.q: A 70-year-old with sepsis has a modestly raised, stable troponin and no chest pain or ECG change. What does this most likely represent?
options: Myocardial injury without evidence of acute infarction
followUp.why: A troponin above the 99th centile without features of ischaemia is myocardial injury. Unstable angina has ischaemic symptoms with no troponin rise; type 1 MI needs evidence of ischaemia; STEMI needs ST elevation.

questions.q: A 64-year-old man has 2 hours of crushing central chest pain. The ECG shows ST elevation in V1–V4. Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.why: V1–V4 look at the septum and anterior wall, which are supplied by the left anterior descending artery. Inferior changes (II, III, aVF) usually mean the right coronary artery; lateral changes (I, aVL, V5–V6) usually the circumflex.
optWhy: The right coronary artery usually causes inferior changes in II, III and aVF.
The circumflex usually causes lateral changes in I, aVL, V5 and V6.
The posterior descending artery supplies the inferior and posterior walls, not the anterior septum.
Correct: anteroseptal ST elevation in V1–V4 points to the left anterior descending artery.
The internal mammary artery is not a native coronary artery; it is used as a bypass graft.
questions.clue: ST elevation in V1–V4.

followUp.q: A man has ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 with reciprocal depression in III and aVF. Which artery is most likely involved?
followUp.why: I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, usually supplied by the circumflex artery. The LAD causes anteroseptal changes and the RCA inferior changes.

questions.q: A 58-year-old woman of Black African family origin, without diabetes, has hypertension confirmed on ambulatory monitoring and needs drug treatment. Under NICE NG136, what is the most appropriate first-line drug class?
questions.why: NICE recommends a calcium-channel blocker at step 1 for adults without type 2 diabetes who are 55 or over or of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin. She meets both criteria.
optWhy: Correct: no type 2 diabetes, and she is 55 or over and of Black African family origin, so a CCB.
A thiazide-like diuretic is used at step 2 or 3, or if a CCB is not suitable.
An ACE inhibitor is step 1 for type 2 diabetes or for under-55s not of Black African or African-Caribbean origin.
Beta-blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension; they appear at step 4.
An ARB has the same step 1 indications as an ACE inhibitor; NICE suggests an ARB rather than an ACE inhibitor when adding a second drug in this group.
questions.clue: Black African family origin, aged 58, no diabetes.

followUp.q: A 45-year-old white man with type 2 diabetes has confirmed stage 1 hypertension needing treatment. What is the first-line class under NICE NG136?
followUp.why: For people with type 2 diabetes, NICE recommends an ACE inhibitor or ARB at step 1 whatever their age or family origin. A CCB would be chosen at 55 or over without diabetes.

questions.q: A 73-year-old man has 3 months of worsening breathlessness and ankle swelling. His GP measures NT-proBNP at 2,600 ng/L. What should happen next, according to NICE NG106?
options: Reassure him that heart failure is unlikely
Start a loop diuretic and review only if symptoms persist
Refer for specialist assessment and echocardiography within 6 weeks
Refer for specialist assessment and echocardiography within 2 weeks
