questions.why: NT-proBNP above 2,000 ng/L means urgent referral for specialist assessment and echocardiography within 2 weeks. Levels between 400 and 2,000 ng/L warrant referral within 6 weeks.
optWhy: A level of 2,600 ng/L is well above the 400 ng/L below which heart failure becomes less likely.
Repeating the test delays diagnosis of a condition with a poor prognosis untreated.
Diuretics may relieve congestion, but diagnosis by echocardiography and specialist assessment still needs to happen urgently.
Six weeks applies to levels of 400–2,000 ng/L.
Correct: above 2,000 ng/L, refer within 2 weeks.
questions.clue: NT-proBNP 2,600 ng/L.
questions.concept: NT-proBNP thresholds for heart failure referral.

followUp.q: A 66-year-old woman with exertional breathlessness has an NT-proBNP of 850 ng/L and is on no treatment. What does NICE advise?
options: Echocardiography and specialist assessment within 6 weeks
followUp.why: 400–2,000 ng/L means referral for specialist assessment and echocardiography within 6 weeks. Above 2,000 would be within 2 weeks; below 400 makes heart failure less likely.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman with new atrial fibrillation has hypertension and had a TIA last year. Calculate her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score and explain the management implication.
markScheme: Age 65–74 scores 1
Female sex scores 1
Hypertension scores 1; previous TIA scores 2
Total = 5
Score of 2 or more: anticoagulation indicated (NICE NG196), with a DOAC generally preferred; assess bleeding risk with ORBIT and address modifiable bleeding risks
questions.modelAnswer: Her score is: age 70 (65–74) = 1, female = 1, hypertension = 1, previous TIA = 2, giving 5. NICE NG196 uses a threshold of 2 or more for offering anticoagulation, so she should be offered an anticoagulant, generally a direct oral anticoagulant rather than warfarin, after discussing benefits and risks with her. Her bleeding risk should be assessed with the ORBIT score, and modifiable bleeding risks (uncontrolled blood pressure, interacting drugs, alcohol) addressed as part of the shared decision. Aspirin alone is not an alternative for stroke prevention.
questions.concept: CHA₂DS₂-VASc scoring and the anticoagulation threshold.

questions.q: Which feature classifies an adult's acute asthma attack as life-threatening rather than acute severe?
questions.why: SpO₂ below 92% is a life-threatening feature. A respiratory rate of 25 or more, heart rate of 110 or more, PEF 33–50% and inability to complete sentences each indicate acute severe asthma.
optWhy: A respiratory rate of 25/min or more is an acute severe feature.
A heart rate of 110/min or more is an acute severe feature.
Correct: SpO₂ below 92% is life-threatening.
PEF of 33–50% is acute severe; life-threatening is below 33%.
Inability to complete sentences in one breath is an acute severe feature.
questions.clue: 'Life-threatening rather than acute severe'.

followUp.q: Which blood gas finding in acute asthma indicates a near-fatal attack?
followUp.why: A raised PaCO₂ defines near-fatal asthma. A low PaCO₂ is expected with hyperventilation; a 'normal' value such as 5.2 kPa is life-threatening; a PaO₂ of 11 kPa on oxygen is not itself a danger sign.

questions.q: A 76-year-old man with pneumonia is alert. Urea 6.2 mmol/L, respiratory rate 32/min, BP 104/58 mmHg. What is his CURB65 score?
questions.why: Confusion 0 (alert); urea 0 (6.2 is not above 7); respiratory rate 1 (30 or more); blood pressure 1 (diastolic 60 or less, even though systolic is not below 90); age 1 (65 or over). Total 3, high risk.
optWhy: 1 counts only age.
2 misses the blood pressure point, forgetting that a diastolic of 60 or less scores even when systolic is 90 or more.
Correct: RR + BP (diastolic 58) + age = 3.
4 wrongly scores the urea of 6.2, which is not above 7 mmol/L.
5 would need confusion and a raised urea as well.
questions.clue: Diastolic 58 mmHg; urea 6.2 mmol/L; RR 32.

followUp.q: A 50-year-old with pneumonia is newly confused, urea 9 mmol/L, RR 22, BP 128/76. What is the CURB65 score?
followUp.why: Confusion 1 and urea above 7 = 1; respiratory rate, blood pressure and age do not score. Total 2, intermediate risk.

questions.q: A 68-year-old with COPD is admitted with an exacerbation. After nebulisers, steroids and controlled oxygen for an hour, the ABG shows pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 8.1 kPa, PaO₂ 7.9 kPa (on 28% oxygen), HCO₃⁻ 29 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Increase to 15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask
Stop oxygen to restore hypoxic drive
Continue current treatment and repeat the gas in 24 hours
questions.why: He has a persistent respiratory acidosis (pH below 7.35 with PaCO₂ above 6.5 kPa) despite optimal medical therapy, which is the indication for NIV under BTS/ICS guidance.
optWhy: Uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen risks worsening hypercapnia and acidosis.
Stopping oxygen is dangerous; he is hypoxaemic. Titrate to 88–92%.
Bicarbonate does not treat a respiratory acidosis; the problem is inadequate ventilation.
Correct: persistent acidosis with hypercapnia despite optimal therapy is the NIV indication.
Waiting 24 hours risks further deterioration; reassess within an hour of any change.
questions.clue: pH 7.29 and PaCO₂ 8.1 kPa persisting after optimal medical therapy.
questions.concept: Indication for NIV in COPD exacerbations.

followUp.q: A man with COPD has pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 6.9 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 31 mmol/L, PaO₂ 8.4 kPa on controlled oxygen. Is NIV indicated?
options: Yes, because PaCO₂ is above 6.5 kPa
Yes, because PaO₂ is below 10 kPa
No, because the pH is not below 7.35: this is compensated chronic hypercapnia
followUp.why: NIV is for respiratory acidosis (pH below 7.35 with PaCO₂ above 6.5 kPa). A normal pH with raised bicarbonate reflects compensated chronic hypercapnia; continue treatment and monitor.

questions.q: A 34-year-old woman has sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness 10 days after knee surgery. Pulse 110, no signs of DVT, no alternative diagnosis more likely; her two-level PE Wells score is 6. CTPA is available within the hour. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Ventilation–perfusion scan only if the chest X-ray is abnormal
questions.why: With a Wells score above 4, PE is 'likely', so NICE NG158 recommends going straight to CTPA (with interim anticoagulation if there is a delay). D-dimer is used when PE is unlikely, because a positive result in a high-probability patient adds little and a negative one cannot safely exclude PE.
optWhy: Correct: PE likely (more than 4), so CTPA.
D-dimer is for patients scoring 4 or fewer; in a likely-PE patient it cannot safely exclude PE.
V/Q scanning is an alternative to CTPA in some groups (e.g. contrast allergy or renal impairment), and is used when the chest X-ray is normal, not abnormal.
Echocardiography may show right heart strain but does not confirm or exclude PE in a stable patient.
Leg ultrasound is for suspected DVT; she has no DVT signs.
questions.clue: Wells score 6.

followUp.q: A 40-year-old with pleuritic pain has a two-level PE Wells score of 1.5. What should be done first?
followUp.why: With 4 or fewer points PE is 'unlikely', so a D-dimer is done first; only if it is positive is CTPA needed. Thrombolysis is reserved for haemodynamically unstable confirmed PE.

questions.q: Explain the difference between type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure, giving a mechanism and an example of each, and explain why oxygen targets differ between patients.
markScheme: Type 1: PaO₂ below 8 kPa with normal or low PaCO₂
Mechanism of type 1: V/Q mismatch or shunt (e.g. pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, PE)
Type 2: PaO₂ below 8 kPa with raised PaCO₂ (above about 6 kPa)
Mechanism of type 2: alveolar hypoventilation (e.g. COPD exacerbation, exhaustion in asthma, opioid toxicity, neuromuscular weakness)
BTS targets: 94–98% for most acutely ill adults; 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic failure, because excess oxygen can worsen hypercapnia (V/Q effects, Haldane effect)
questions.modelAnswer: Both types have a PaO₂ below 8 kPa. In type 1 the PaCO₂ is normal or low. It is caused by V/Q mismatch or shunt: blood passes alveoli that are poorly ventilated, as in pneumonia, pulmonary oedema or PE. CO₂ can still be cleared by better-ventilated areas, and hyperventilation often lowers it. In type 2 the PaCO₂ is raised because overall alveolar ventilation is inadequate, as in a COPD exacerbation, an exhausted asthmatic, opioid toxicity or neuromuscular weakness. The BTS recommends target saturations of 94–98% for most acutely ill adults, but 88–92% for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as many with COPD, because giving them too much oxygen can raise PaCO₂ further by releasing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (worsening V/Q mismatch) and through the Haldane effect. Oxygen is titrated to the target, not withheld.
questions.concept: Mechanisms of respiratory failure and oxygen targets.

questions.q: Which finding in ascitic fluid best supports a diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
options: Ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250 cells/mm³
questions.why: SBP is diagnosed by an ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250 cells/mm³ without a surgically treatable source, whether or not the culture is positive.
optWhy: A high albumin gradient indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites, not infection.
High ascitic protein suggests causes such as heart failure or malignancy, and does not diagnose infection.
Correct: neutrophil count of at least 250 cells/mm³ defines SBP.
Bilirubin reflects liver function, not ascitic infection.
A raised ascitic amylase suggests pancreatic ascites.
questions.clue: 'Best supports' SBP, a question about ascitic fluid.

followUp.q: A man with cirrhosis and ascites becomes more confused, with a mildly raised creatinine but no abdominal pain. What should be done first?
followUp.why: SBP can present only with encephalopathy or worsening renal function, so any deterioration in a patient with ascites should prompt a diagnostic tap. Increasing diuretics could worsen renal function.

questions.q: A 47-year-old man has one episode of coffee-ground vomiting. He is haemodynamically stable. Before endoscopy, which management is recommended by NICE CG141 for suspected non-variceal bleeding?
options: Start an IV proton pump inhibitor immediately
Do not give acid-suppression drugs before endoscopy
questions.why: NICE CG141 advises against acid-suppression drugs before endoscopy in suspected non-variceal bleeding, because they do not improve key outcomes. PPIs are given after endoscopy when stigmata of recent haemorrhage are seen.
optWhy: Pre-endoscopy PPIs are not recommended for suspected non-variceal bleeding.
Terlipressin is for suspected variceal bleeding.
Correct: no acid suppression before endoscopy for suspected non-variceal bleeding.
Tranexamic acid is not a routine recommendation in this guideline.
TIPS is for uncontrolled variceal bleeding.
questions.clue: Stable, suspected non-variceal bleed, before endoscopy.
questions.concept: Acid suppression timing in upper GI bleeding.

followUp.q: At endoscopy a duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel is treated. What does NICE recommend afterwards?
followUp.why: PPIs are offered after endoscopy to patients with non-variceal bleeding and stigmata of recent haemorrhage. Terlipressin is for varices.

questions.q: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis vomits a large volume of fresh blood. Pulse 124, BP 86/50. Alongside resuscitation, what drug treatment should be given at presentation?
questions.why: NICE CG141 recommends terlipressin for suspected variceal bleeding at presentation and prophylactic antibiotics for suspected or confirmed variceal bleeding, followed by endoscopic band ligation of oesophageal varices.
optWhy: Correct: terlipressin plus prophylactic antibiotics at presentation.
A PPI alone does not treat variceal bleeding.
Non-selective beta-blockers are used for prevention of variceal bleeding, not in a shocked patient during an acute bleed.
Lactulose treats or prevents encephalopathy; it does not stop the bleed.
Vitamin K does not correct the coagulopathy of liver disease quickly and does not treat varices.
questions.clue: Alcohol-related cirrhosis with a large haematemesis and shock.
questions.concept: Initial drug management of variceal bleeding.

followUp.q: A patient's oesophageal variceal bleeding continues despite band ligation. What should be considered next?
followUp.why: NICE CG141 advises considering TIPS when oesophageal variceal bleeding is not controlled by band ligation, because it decompresses the portal system.

questions.q: A 26-year-old has 6 weeks of diarrhoea with weight loss and a perianal fistula. Colonoscopy shows patchy ulceration with normal segments in between, and biopsies show transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Skip lesions, transmural inflammation, granulomas and fistulae are characteristic of Crohn's disease. UC is continuous from the rectum, mucosal, without granulomas or fistulae.
optWhy: UC is continuous, superficial and does not form fistulae or granulomas.
Coeliac disease affects the small bowel mucosa (villous atrophy) and does not cause colonic ulceration or fistulae.
Correct: skip lesions, transmural inflammation, granulomas and a fistula.
IBS has no ulceration or histological inflammation.
Ischaemic colitis affects older people with vascular disease and does not cause granulomas or perianal fistulae.
questions.clue: Skip lesions, granulomas and a perianal fistula.

followUp.q: A 30-year-old has bloody diarrhoea. Colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation from the rectum to the splenic flexure, confined to the mucosa. Which associated condition should you be alert to?
followUp.why: Continuous mucosal disease from the rectum is UC, which is associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis. Fistulae, strictures and ileal disease are features of Crohn's.

questions.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis has 9 bloody stools a day, pulse 104 and temperature 38.1 °C. Classify the flare and list four immediate management steps.
markScheme: Acute severe UC by Truelove and Witts (more than 6 stools a day plus systemic features)
Admit; IV corticosteroids
Stool cultures including C. difficile toxin; bloods (FBC, CRP, U&E, albumin)
Abdominal X-ray for colonic dilatation (toxic megacolon); flexible sigmoidoscopy
VTE prophylaxis, fluids and electrolyte correction; joint gastroenterology and colorectal surgical review, with rescue therapy or colectomy considered if no response by about day 3
questions.modelAnswer: This is acute severe ulcerative colitis: more than 6 bloody stools a day with systemic toxicity (tachycardia above 90 and fever). The patient should be admitted. Immediate steps are IV corticosteroids; stool cultures and C. difficile toxin testing to exclude infection; bloods including full blood count, CRP, urea and electrolytes and albumin; an abdominal X-ray to look for colonic dilatation suggesting toxic megacolon, and flexible sigmoidoscopy; VTE prophylaxis, because IBD flares are prothrombotic; IV fluids with potassium correction; and early joint care with the colorectal surgeons. Response is reassessed at about day 3, when rescue medical therapy or colectomy is considered if there is no adequate improvement.
questions.concept: Recognition and initial management of acute severe UC.

questions.q: Within what time from symptom onset does NICE recommend intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke, once haemorrhage has been excluded?
questions.why: NICE NG128 recommends alteplase as soon as possible within 4.5 hours of onset, and TA990 recommends tenecteplase within the same window, once intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded.
optWhy: One hour is a door-to-needle target in some services, not the treatment window.
Correct: 4.5 hours from onset.
Twelve hours is the window for primary PCI in STEMI, not stroke thrombolysis.
Twenty-four hours is the outer limit for thrombectomy in selected patients with salvageable brain on imaging.
Forty-eight hours has no role in stroke reperfusion decisions.
questions.clue: 'Intravenous thrombolysis'.

followUp.q: A patient with a confirmed proximal anterior circulation occlusion was last known well 10 hours ago. Imaging shows a small core and large salvageable area. What does NICE allow?
followUp.why: NICE NG128 offers thrombectomy between 6 and 24 hours after the patient was last known well if imaging shows potential to salvage brain tissue. The thrombolysis window (4.5 hours) has passed.

questions.q: A 68-year-old woman has sudden weakness of her right face and arm, difficulty finding words, and a right homonymous hemianopia. What is the Bamford classification?
questions.why: All three TACS criteria are present: unilateral motor deficit of at least two of face, arm and leg; homonymous hemianopia; higher cortical dysfunction (dysphasia). Right-sided signs with dysphasia localise to the left hemisphere.
optWhy: A PACS has only two of the three criteria; here all three are present.
An isolated hemianopia can be posterior, but with dysphasia and weakness this is anterior circulation.
Right-sided weakness and dysphasia come from the left hemisphere, not the right.
Lacunar strokes have no cortical signs such as dysphasia or field loss.
Correct: all three criteria, left hemisphere.
questions.clue: Face and arm weakness, dysphasia and a homonymous hemianopia.

followUp.q: A man has pure weakness of the left face, arm and leg, with no sensory loss, no field defect and normal speech and cognition. What is the most likely classification?
followUp.why: A pure motor stroke without cortical signs is a lacunar syndrome, typically from a small vessel infarct in the internal capsule.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman develops a sudden severe occipital headache, maximal within a minute, while lifting weights. A non-contrast CT head performed 9 hours after onset is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Lumbar puncture now, as soon as possible
Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after headache onset to look for xanthochromia
questions.why: CT accuracy for SAH is highest within 6 hours of onset, so a normal CT at 9 hours does not exclude it. NICE NG228 advises allowing at least 12 hours after onset before lumbar puncture, so xanthochromia (bilirubin from red cell breakdown) can be detected on spectrophotometry.
optWhy: Discharging without excluding SAH could miss a rebleed, which carries high mortality.
An LP at 9 hours is too early for xanthochromia to have formed reliably.
Correct: LP at least 12 hours after onset for xanthochromia.
A delayed MRI does not answer the urgent question.
A repeat CT becomes less sensitive with time, not more.
questions.clue: Thunderclap headache, CT normal at 9 hours.

followUp.q: A man's thunderclap headache began 3 hours ago and CT clearly shows blood in the basal cisterns. What next?
options: CT angiography to find the aneurysm and referral to neurosurgery
followUp.why: CT has confirmed SAH, so an LP is unnecessary. The next step is to identify the source (CT angiography) and involve the neurosurgical team to secure the aneurysm; thrombolysis would be dangerous.

questions.q: A 32-year-old with epilepsy has been having a generalised tonic–clonic seizure for 6 minutes in the emergency department. IV access is established and capillary glucose is 5.6 mmol/L. What should be given first?
questions.why: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated once a seizure has lasted 5 minutes. With IV access and resuscitation facilities available, NICE NG217 recommends an IV benzodiazepine first, repeated once if the seizure continues 5–10 minutes later, then a second-line drug.
optWhy: Levetiracetam is a second-line option after two benzodiazepine doses.
Correct: benzodiazepine first.
General anaesthesia is a third-line option under expert guidance.
Glucose is normal, so it would not treat the cause here.
Phenobarbital is third line.
questions.clue: Seizing for 6 minutes with IV access; glucose normal.

followUp.q: The same patient is still seizing after two doses of IV benzodiazepine. Which is an appropriate next drug under NICE NG217?
options: IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate
IV magnesium in a non-pregnant patient
followUp.why: After two benzodiazepine doses, NICE recommends an IV second-line agent: levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate (valproate following MHRA safety measures). Magnesium is for eclampsia.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man has 4 days of ascending weakness in his legs and now his arms, 2 weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Reflexes are absent. Give the likely diagnosis, two supporting investigations, how you would monitor him and the specific treatment.
markScheme: Guillain–Barré syndrome (post-infectious, e.g. Campylobacter)
Nerve conduction studies (demyelinating or axonal neuropathy)
Lumbar puncture: raised protein with normal white cell count (may be normal early)
Serial forced vital capacity (not peak flow), plus cardiac monitoring for autonomic instability; early critical care referral if FVC falls
IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange; corticosteroids are not indicated; supportive care and VTE prophylaxis
questions.modelAnswer: The likely diagnosis is Guillain–Barré syndrome, an immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy often triggered by an infection such as Campylobacter. Nerve conduction studies support it, and a lumbar puncture typically shows raised protein with a normal white cell count, although it can be normal in the first week. He should have regular forced vital capacity measurements, not peak flow, because facial and bulbar weakness make peak flow unreliable, plus monitoring of heart rate and blood pressure for autonomic instability and assessment of swallowing. A falling FVC should prompt early critical care referral. Specific treatment is IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange; corticosteroids are not effective. Supportive care includes VTE prophylaxis, pain control and physiotherapy.
questions.concept: Diagnosis and monitoring of Guillain–Barré syndrome.

questions.q: Which set of results meets the JBDS 2023 diagnostic criteria for diabetic ketoacidosis?
options: Glucose 9 mmol/L in a person without diabetes, ketones 4.0 mmol/L, pH 7.25
Glucose 38 mmol/L, ketones 0.8 mmol/L, osmolality 340 mOsm/kg
Glucose 22 mmol/L, ketones 3.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L
Glucose 15 mmol/L, ketones 3.4 mmol/L, pH 7.36, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L
questions.why: DKA needs all three: ketones above 3.0 mmol/L, glucose above 11 mmol/L or known diabetes, and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3. Only the set with ketones 3.8, glucose 22 and bicarbonate 12 meets all three.
optWhy: Ketones of 1.2 mmol/L and pH 7.34 do not meet the criteria.
Glucose 9 mmol/L without known diabetes fails the glucose criterion (consider other causes of ketoacidosis).
Low ketones with high osmolality suggest HHS rather than DKA.
Correct: all three criteria met.
Ketosis without acidosis (pH 7.36, bicarbonate 22) does not meet the acidosis criterion.
questions.clue: 'Meets the JBDS 2023 diagnostic criteria'.

followUp.q: Which finding is a JBDS marker of severe DKA prompting senior review and consideration of level 2 care?
followUp.why: Hypokalaemia (below 3.5 mmol/L) on admission is a severity marker. Ketones above 6, bicarbonate below 5 and pH below 7.0 are others; glucose level is not a severity marker.

questions.q: A 79-year-old with type 2 diabetes has a week of confusion. Glucose 46 mmol/L, sodium 150, urea 18, ketones 0.9 mmol/L, venous pH 7.36. She looks very dry. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin and oral fluids
IV fluid resuscitation, without insulin initially
questions.why: Calculated osmolality is 2 × 150 + 46 + 18 = 364 mOsm/kg with low ketones and no acidosis: HHS. Fluids come first and lower glucose on their own; insulin is started only if there is significant ketonaemia or glucose stops falling, to avoid a rapid fall in osmolality.
optWhy: Insulin without fluid can cause circulatory collapse and a rapid osmolality fall.
There is no significant acidosis to treat.
She is too unwell for subcutaneous insulin and oral fluids.
Correct: fluids first in HHS.
Hypernatraemia here reflects water loss; she needs fluid, not restriction.
questions.clue: Glucose 46, osmolality about 364, ketones 0.9, pH 7.36, older person with type 2 diabetes.

followUp.q: Two hours into fluid treatment for HHS her glucose has stopped falling and ketones are now 1.4 mmol/L. What is the appropriate change?
followUp.why: Insulin is started in HHS when glucose stops falling with fluids or significant ketonaemia develops, at a low rate to avoid rapid osmolality changes. Fluids continue; bicarbonate and glucose are not indicated.

questions.q: A 34-year-old who has taken oral prednisolone for 2 years stopped it suddenly a week ago. She is admitted with vomiting, BP 82/48, sodium 128 mmol/L and glucose 3.4 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: IV hydrocortisone and IV fluids immediately
Arrange a short Synacthen test before treatment
questions.why: This is adrenal crisis from suppression of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis after stopping long-term steroids. Parenteral hydrocortisone and IV fluids are given immediately; a cortisol sample can be taken, but treatment must not wait for results.
optWhy: Correct: immediate parenteral hydrocortisone and fluids.
Testing first delays life-saving treatment.
She is hypoglycaemic; insulin would worsen it.
She is shocked and vomiting; oral steroid and discharge are unsafe.
Hyponatraemia here is from cortisol deficiency and volume loss; she needs fluids.
questions.clue: Long-term steroids stopped abruptly; hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia.
questions.concept: Recognition and treatment of adrenal crisis.

followUp.q: Which electrolyte pattern most suggests primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)?
followUp.why: Aldosterone deficiency causes salt wasting (hyponatraemia) and potassium retention (hyperkalaemia). Hypernatraemia with hypokalaemia suggests mineralocorticoid excess, as does hypokalaemic alkalosis.

questions.q: A 52-year-old with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes had a myocardial infarction 2 years ago. eGFR is 72 and she tolerates metformin. Under NICE NG28 (2026), which initial combination is recommended?
options: Modified-release metformin, an SGLT2 inhibitor and subcutaneous semaglutide
questions.why: For people with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, NICE NG28 (2026) recommends modified-release metformin, an SGLT2 inhibitor and subcutaneous semaglutide for cardiovascular, renal and glycaemic benefit.
optWhy: Metformin alone is no longer the initial NICE recommendation; an SGLT2 inhibitor is added from the start.
Correct: metformin, SGLT2 inhibitor and semaglutide for established atherosclerotic disease.
Sulfonylureas are not part of the recommended initial combinations and carry hypoglycaemia risk.
Insulin is not first-line for a newly diagnosed, asymptomatic adult with type 2 diabetes.
DPP-4 inhibitor monotherapy is considered in specific situations such as very low eGFR or frailty with risk from SGLT2 inhibitors.
questions.clue: Previous MI (established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease).
questions.concept: NICE NG28 (2026) initial treatment by clinical profile.

followUp.q: An 84-year-old with frailty, recurrent dizziness and low blood pressure is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Under NG28 (2026), what is the key caution about SGLT2 inhibitors?
options: Offer them only if frailty does not put the person at risk of adverse events such as volume depletion or hypotension
They must be combined with insulin
followUp.why: NICE says to offer modified-release metformin in frailty and to offer an SGLT2 inhibitor only if frailty does not put the person at risk of adverse events such as volume depletion or hypotension; with such risk, alternatives like a DPP-4 inhibitor are considered.

questions.q: Explain why serum potassium may be normal or high at presentation in DKA and why it falls during treatment. State the practical implication.
markScheme: Insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells, so serum potassium can be normal or high
Osmotic diuresis and vomiting cause total-body potassium depletion
Insulin drives potassium into cells (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) and fluids dilute it, so serum potassium falls during treatment
Correction of acidosis also moves potassium into cells
Implication: monitor potassium frequently; add potassium to fluids once it is 5.5 mmol/L or lower and urine is passed; hypokalaemia on admission is a severity marker
questions.modelAnswer: In DKA insulin deficiency, high osmolality and acidosis all move potassium out of cells into the blood, so the measured serum level can be normal or even high. At the same time the osmotic diuresis and vomiting have caused a large loss of total-body potassium. Treatment reverses the shift: insulin stimulates the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and drives potassium into cells, correcting acidosis has the same effect, and IV fluids dilute the remaining potassium. Serum potassium therefore falls, sometimes to dangerous levels that cause arrhythmias. In practice potassium is checked frequently, potassium is added to fluids once the level is 5.5 mmol/L or less and the patient is passing urine, and a low potassium at admission is treated as a marker of severe DKA needing senior review.
questions.concept: Potassium shifts in DKA and its treatment.

questions.q: Which treatment for hyperkalaemia stabilises the myocardium but does not lower serum potassium?
questions.why: IV calcium protects the heart against arrhythmia by restoring the gap between resting and threshold potential, but potassium is unchanged. Insulin and salbutamol shift potassium into cells; binders and dialysis remove it.
optWhy: Insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells, lowering serum levels.
Salbutamol shifts potassium into cells (as an adjunct).
Dialysis removes potassium directly.
Potassium binders remove potassium from the body via the gut.
Correct: calcium stabilises the membrane without lowering potassium.
questions.clue: 'Does not lower serum potassium'.

followUp.q: Which treatment shifts potassium into cells by stimulating the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase?
followUp.why: Insulin (with glucose to prevent hypoglycaemia) stimulates the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Calcium protects the heart; patiromer removes potassium; stopping spironolactone removes a cause.

questions.q: A 78-year-old's creatinine has risen from a baseline of 95 µmol/L to 300 µmol/L over 5 days. Urine output is maintained. What is the KDIGO stage?
options: Not AKI, because urine output is normal
questions.why: 300 ÷ 95 ≈ 3.2 times baseline, which is 3 times or more: stage 3. Creatinine criteria alone are enough; a normal urine output does not exclude AKI.
optWhy: Creatinine criteria alone define AKI; urine output need not fall.
Stage 1 is 1.5–1.9 times baseline or a rise of 26.5 µmol/L within 48 hours.
Stage 2 is 2.0–2.9 times baseline; this is above 3.
Correct: about 3.2 times baseline is stage 3.
A rise over 5 days from a known baseline is acute, not CKD.
questions.clue: Creatinine 95 → 300 µmol/L over 5 days.

followUp.q: A patient's creatinine rises from 110 to 140 µmol/L over 36 hours. Is this AKI and what stage?
options: Stage 1: a rise of 26.5 µmol/L or more within 48 hours
followUp.why: The rise is 30 µmol/L within 48 hours, which meets the stage 1 absolute criterion even though the ratio (1.27) is below 1.5.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man has potassium 6.8 mmol/L on a non-haemolysed sample. The ECG shows broad QRS complexes. What should be given first?
questions.why: With ECG changes, the first step is to protect the myocardium with IV calcium; then shift potassium into cells with insulin–glucose (salbutamol as an adjunct) and remove it with a binder or dialysis.
optWhy: Salbutamol is an adjunct in severe hyperkalaemia, not to be used alone.
Binders act over hours and do not protect the heart now.
Correct: IV calcium first when the ECG is abnormal.
UKKA does not recommend routine IV bicarbonate for acute hyperkalaemia.
Loop diuretics have no place as first treatment and may worsen AKI if the patient is dry.
questions.clue: Potassium 6.8 with broad QRS.

followUp.q: After IV calcium and insulin–glucose for severe hyperkalaemia, what must be monitored closely?
options: Blood glucose and potassium (for hypoglycaemia and rebound)
followUp.why: Insulin–glucose can cause hypoglycaemia, and the shift of potassium is temporary, so potassium can rebound. UKKA advises close monitoring of both.

questions.q: An 82-year-old with heart failure has 4 days of diarrhoea. He takes ramipril, furosemide, spironolactone and ibuprofen. Creatinine 245 µmol/L (baseline 98), BP 96/60, JVP not visible. Which is the most important immediate drug action?
options: Withhold ramipril, furosemide, spironolactone and ibuprofen
Continue all medicines and recheck in a week
questions.why: This is AKI stage 2 (245 ÷ 98 = 2.5) that is likely pre-renal from volume loss. The ACE inhibitor, diuretics and NSAID all impair renal perfusion or cause potassium retention, so they should be withheld while volume is restored, and reviewed for restarting when he recovers.
optWhy: More diuretic would worsen volume depletion and AKI.
Correct: withhold the nephrotoxic and risky drugs.
SGLT2 inhibitors are not started during acute illness with volume depletion.
Continuing them risks worsening AKI and hyperkalaemia.
Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic and there is no indication.
questions.clue: Diarrhoea, low BP, dry, on ACE inhibitor, diuretics and an NSAID.

followUp.q: A man with AKI has a palpable, tender bladder and has not passed urine for 12 hours. What is the most useful immediate step?
followUp.why: A palpable bladder suggests post-renal (obstructive) AKI, commonly from prostatic obstruction. Relieving it with a catheter is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

questions.q: A 78-year-old's creatinine has risen from 95 to 300 µmol/L over 5 days. Stage the AKI and list four investigations that help identify the cause, saying what each looks for.
markScheme: Stage 3 (more than 3 × baseline: 300 ÷ 95 ≈ 3.2)
Urine dipstick (before catheter if possible): blood and protein suggest glomerulonephritis; leucocytes and nitrites suggest infection
Renal tract ultrasound: hydronephrosis from obstruction (and kidney size)
Bloods: potassium, venous gas for acidosis, FBC, CRP, CK (rhabdomyolysis), cultures if septic
Medication review and fluid balance/volume assessment for pre-renal causes and nephrotoxins
questions.modelAnswer: Creatinine has risen to about 3.2 times baseline (300 ÷ 95), so this is KDIGO stage 3 AKI. To find the cause: a urine dipstick, ideally before catheterisation, where blood and protein point to a glomerular cause (and urine ACR or PCR can quantify protein), while leucocytes and nitrites suggest infection. A renal tract ultrasound looks for hydronephrosis from obstruction and small kidneys suggesting underlying CKD. Blood tests: potassium and a venous gas for life-threatening complications, full blood count and CRP for sepsis, creatine kinase for rhabdomyolysis, and blood cultures if septic; a nephritic screen if glomerulonephritis is suspected. A careful review of medicines (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, aminoglycosides) and of volume status and fluid balance identifies pre-renal causes and nephrotoxins.

questions.q: Under the Royal College of Physicians NEWS2 chart, which aggregate score is the key threshold for an urgent response?
options: Any score of 2 or more in a single parameter
questions.why: An aggregate of 5–6 is medium risk, the key threshold for an urgent response by a clinician or team skilled in acute illness. 7 or more is high risk (urgent or emergency response); a single red score of 3 needs an urgent ward-based response.
optWhy: 1–2 is within the low-risk band (0–4) with a ward-based response.
3–4 is still low risk unless a single parameter scores 3.
A single parameter scoring 3 (not 2) triggers an urgent ward-based response.
Correct: 5–6 is the key threshold for an urgent response.
Temperature alone scores at most 2 for hyperthermia (39.1 °C or more), so 38.0 °C alone does not trigger escalation.
questions.clue: 'Key threshold for an urgent response'.

followUp.q: A patient has a NEWS2 aggregate of 2, but the respiratory rate alone scores 3. What does the RCP chart advise?
followUp.why: A single red score of 3 in any parameter triggers an urgent ward-based response even when the total is low.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman develops stridor, widespread urticaria and a BP of 78/40 within minutes of a wasp sting. What is the most important first drug treatment?
options: IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh
questions.why: This is anaphylaxis with airway and circulatory compromise. IM adrenaline into the anterolateral middle third of the thigh is the first treatment, repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement, alongside oxygen and IV fluids for shock.
optWhy: Antihistamines are not part of initial emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.
Routine corticosteroids are no longer advised for initial treatment.
Correct: IM adrenaline first.
Salbutamol may help residual bronchospasm but does not treat stridor or shock.
Oral antihistamines are far too slow and do not address airway or circulation.
questions.clue: Stridor and hypotension after a sting.

followUp.q: The same patient has had two appropriate IM adrenaline doses 5 minutes apart and IV fluids but remains hypotensive. What is the next step?
options: Adrenaline infusion with expert (critical care) support
A third IM dose and discharge after 2 hours
followUp.why: Persisting cardiovascular problems after two IM doses define refractory anaphylaxis, treated with an adrenaline infusion under expert guidance alongside further fluids.

questions.q: A 58-year-old collapses on the ward. He is unresponsive with no signs of life, and the monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. One shock has been given and CPR resumed. According to the RCUK 2025 adult ALS algorithm, when are adrenaline and amiodarone first given?
options: Only if the rhythm becomes asystole
Amiodarone is not used in VF
questions.why: In shockable rhythms, adrenaline and amiodarone are given after the third shock; adrenaline is then repeated every 3–5 minutes. In non-shockable rhythms adrenaline is given as soon as possible.
optWhy: Giving drugs before the second shock is not the algorithm for shockable rhythms.
Asystole is a non-shockable rhythm where adrenaline is given as soon as possible, but that does not apply to VF.
A further amiodarone dose may be given after the fifth shock; it is not when the first doses are given.
Correct: after the third shock.
Amiodarone is part of the shockable pathway.
questions.clue: VF, shockable rhythm.
questions.concept: Drug timing in the ALS algorithm.

followUp.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has organised electrical activity on the monitor but no pulse. What is the priority drug action?
options: Wait three cycles before any drug
Adrenaline as soon as possible, with CPR and a search for reversible causes
followUp.why: Pulseless electrical activity is non-shockable. Adrenaline is given as soon as possible with high-quality CPR, and reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts) are sought.

questions.q: A 22-year-old says she took paracetamol tablets repeatedly over the past 36 hours, but cannot say how many or when. She is alert, with normal observations. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Wait for a 4-hour paracetamol level and plot it on the nomogram
Give activated charcoal and discharge if well
Start acetylcysteine without delay, with bloods including paracetamol level, LFTs and INR
Reassure her because she is asymptomatic
questions.why: This is a staggered overdose with uncertain timing, so the treatment line cannot be applied. Acetylcysteine is started without delay, and bloods (paracetamol, LFTs, INR, U&E, venous gas) guide how long treatment continues.
optWhy: The nomogram is valid only for a single ingestion at a known time.
Charcoal is only useful soon after a single ingestion; discharge would miss liver injury.
Correct: start acetylcysteine without delay in staggered or uncertain-time overdoses.
Paracetamol toxicity is often asymptomatic early, so being well does not exclude liver injury.
Naloxone reverses opioids, not paracetamol.
questions.clue: Repeated ingestion over 36 hours, timing unknown.

followUp.q: A man took a single overdose of paracetamol at a known time. His level at 4 hours is above the single treatment line (100 mg/L at 4 hours). He has no risk factors. What should happen?
options: No treatment because he has no risk factors
Repeat the level at 12 hours before deciding
followUp.why: Acetylcysteine is given to anyone on or above the treatment line, regardless of risk factors.

questions.q: A patient has a paracetamol overdose taken in multiple tablets over 2 days. Explain how this changes management compared with a single acute overdose, and why.
markScheme: Single acute overdose at known time: measure level at 4 hours or later and plot on the single treatment line (100 mg/L at 4 hours)
Treat with acetylcysteine if on or above the line, regardless of risk factors
Staggered overdose: the nomogram is invalid because the level cannot be related to a single time of ingestion
So start acetylcysteine without delay
Take paracetamol level, LFTs, INR, U&E and venous gas to guide continuation; seek specialist (TOXBASE/poisons) advice and assess mental health and safeguarding
questions.modelAnswer: In a single acute overdose at a known time, the plasma paracetamol level is measured at 4 hours or later and plotted on the single treatment line, which joins 100 mg/L at 4 hours to lower values later. Acetylcysteine is given if the level is on or above the line, whatever the patient's risk factors. In a staggered overdose over 2 days the level cannot be interpreted against a single time of ingestion, so the nomogram is not valid. Acetylcysteine is therefore started without delay. Bloods (paracetamol level, liver tests, INR, renal function and a venous gas) are still taken to judge liver injury and guide how long treatment continues, with advice from TOXBASE or the poisons service. A psychiatric and safeguarding assessment follows once the patient is medically fit.

questions.q: A 61-year-old man presents with 90 minutes of central crushing chest pain radiating to his jaw. He smokes and has type 2 diabetes. ECG: 3 mm ST elevation in II, III and aVF with ST depression in I and aVL. The nearest PCI centre is 40 minutes away. (a) Interpret the ECG and explain the pathophysiology. (b) Outline immediate management, applying current NICE criteria. (c) What complications should you anticipate in the first 48 hours, and why? (d) Outline secondary prevention principles (no doses).
markScheme: (a) Inferior STEMI with reciprocal lateral depression; usual culprit the right coronary artery
(a) Plaque rupture/erosion with occlusive thrombus causing transmural ischaemia; time-dependent myocyte death
(b) ABCDE, oxygen only if hypoxic (BTS targets), analgesia, antiplatelet therapy; do not wait for troponin
(b) NICE NG185: within 12 hours and PCI deliverable within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could be given, so primary PCI; fibrinolysis only if this cannot be met
(c) Bradycardia and AV block (RCA usually supplies the AV node); right ventricular infarction with hypotension (right-sided leads, avoid nitrates and give fluid cautiously)
(c) Arrhythmias (VF, VT), heart failure, mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture, VSD) and pericarditis
(d) Antiplatelet therapy, statin, ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation, diabetes and BP control
Clear structure, accurate guideline use, no doses
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ST elevation in II, III and aVF localises to the inferior wall, usually supplied by the right coronary artery; reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL supports a true infarct rather than pericarditis. The usual mechanism is rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque, exposing thrombogenic material so that platelets aggregate and an occlusive thrombus forms. Complete occlusion causes transmural ischaemia, seen as ST elevation, and myocytes begin to die within minutes, so delay costs muscle.

(b) He is assessed with ABCDE, given oxygen only if he is hypoxic (BTS target 94–98%), analgesia and antiplatelet therapy. STEMI is diagnosed on the ECG with the history, so reperfusion is not delayed for troponin. Under NICE NG185, primary PCI is preferred when the patient presents within 12 hours of onset and PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could have been given. He is 90 minutes from onset and 40 minutes from a PCI centre, so he should be transferred directly for primary PCI. Fibrinolysis would be offered only if PCI could not be delivered in that time.

(c) Because the right coronary artery usually supplies the AV node, bradycardia and heart block are common after inferior MI. Right ventricular involvement (ST elevation in V4R) causes hypotension with clear lungs; these patients are preload-dependent, so nitrates are avoided and fluid is given cautiously. Any MI can be complicated by VF or VT, especially early, as well as heart failure, mechanical complications such as papillary muscle rupture (acute mitral regurgitation) or ventricular septal rupture, and pericarditis.

(d) Secondary prevention combines antiplatelet therapy, a high-intensity statin, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker, plus cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation, and tight blood pressure and diabetes control. No doses are given here; follow the current BNF and local protocols.
questions.concept: STEMI recognition, reperfusion criteria and complications.

questions.q: Essay: 'Early recognition saves more lives in acute medicine than any single treatment.' Discuss with reference to NEWS2, sepsis, anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest.
markScheme: Explains the ABCDE approach and the value of structured reassessment
Describes NEWS2 parameters and RCP thresholds (single 3, 5–6, 7 or more) and how they link to responses
Sepsis: Sepsis-3 definitions; NICE NG253 uses NEWS2 to set antibiotic timing (1, 3, 6 hours) and lactate above 2 mmol/L as high risk
Anaphylaxis: rapid recognition of airway/breathing/circulation problems allows early IM adrenaline; delay or antihistamine-first care worsens outcomes
Cardiac arrest: many in-hospital arrests are preceded by deterioration; early warning and escalation can prevent arrest; ALS and reversible causes
Balances the argument: recognition must be linked to an effective response and treatment (antibiotics, source control, adrenaline, defibrillation)
Considers limitations: NEWS2 not validated in pregnancy or under 16s; clinical concern should override a low score; alarm fatigue
Structured, evidence-based conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Acute medicine is a race against physiology, and much of the harm in hospital comes not from a lack of treatment but from failure to recognise deterioration in time. The statement is largely true, but recognition only saves lives when it is tied to a timely, effective response.

The ABCDE approach gives a structure for assessing and treating problems in order of threat to life, with reassessment after every intervention. NEWS2 adds objective tracking. It scores respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen, systolic blood pressure, pulse, consciousness (where new confusion scores 3) and temperature. The Royal College of Physicians links scores to responses: a single parameter scoring 3 needs an urgent ward-based response, 5–6 is the key threshold for an urgent response, and 7 or more needs an urgent or emergency response including staff with critical care skills. The value of the score is that it turns subtle, scattered changes into a common language for escalation.

Sepsis shows why this matters. Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, and septic shock as needing vasopressors to keep mean arterial pressure at 65 mmHg or more with a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluids. NICE NG253 uses NEWS2 to stratify adults in acute hospitals: with suspected infection, a score of 7 or more means senior review and antibiotics within 1 hour, 5–6 within 3 hours, and 1–4 within 6 hours if indicated, with a lactate above 2 mmol/L treated as high risk. Here, recognition directly sets treatment timing. Yet antibiotics alone are not enough: source control, such as draining an abscess or repairing a leaking anastomosis, is often decisive.

In anaphylaxis, recognition and treatment are almost the same act. Sudden airway, breathing or circulation problems after a trigger must be recognised quickly so that IM adrenaline is given into the anterolateral thigh and repeated after 5 minutes if needed (RCUK 2021). Giving antihistamines first, or waiting for skin signs, delays the one drug that reverses vasodilatation, capillary leak and bronchospasm.

Cardiac arrest is often the end of a period of unrecognised deterioration. Early warning and escalation can prevent some arrests altogether. Once arrest occurs, recognition of the rhythm matters: shockable rhythms need early defibrillation, with adrenaline and amiodarone after the third shock, while PEA and asystole need adrenaline as soon as possible and a search for reversible causes (RCUK 2025).

There are limits. NEWS2 is not designed for pregnancy or for children, a low score must not override clinical concern, and frequent alarms can cause fatigue. Recognition without a capable response team, or without effective treatment, achieves little. In conclusion, early recognition is the step that makes every other treatment possible, but lives are saved by the whole chain: recognise, escalate, treat and reassess.
questions.concept: Recognition and escalation of the deteriorating patient.

cases.title: Crushing chest pain at the bus stop

steps.text: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who smokes is brought in by ambulance with 90 minutes of central crushing chest pain radiating to his jaw, with sweating. Pulse 96, BP 138/84, SpO₂ 97% on air.

ask.q: What is the single most important immediate investigation?
ask.why: The 12-lead ECG decides whether this is a STEMI needing immediate reperfusion. Troponin takes time and must not delay reperfusion when the ECG shows STEMI; chest X-ray and D-dimer address other differentials but are not the first priority.

steps.text: The ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in II, III and aVF with ST depression in I and aVL. The nearest PCI centre is 40 minutes away and can take him now.

ask.q: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy under NICE NG185?
options: Medical management and angiography within 72 hours
ask.why: He presented within 12 hours of onset and PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given, so primary PCI is preferred. Fibrinolysis is for when PCI cannot be delivered in that time. Angiography within 72 hours is the NSTEMI pathway for intermediate or higher risk.

steps.text: On the way to the lab his heart rate falls to 40/min and his BP to 84/50. Right-sided leads show ST elevation in V4R.

ask.q: What best explains the new findings?
options: Inferior MI involving the right ventricle and the AV node
Vasovagal syncope unrelated to the MI
ask.why: The right coronary artery usually supplies the inferior wall, the right ventricle and (in most people) the AV node, so inferior MI can cause right ventricular infarction (hypotension, ST elevation in V4R) and bradycardia or heart block. He has not received fibrinolysis, and anterior extension would show in V1–V4.

steps.text: Outcome: the right coronary artery is opened at primary PCI and his rhythm and blood pressure recover. Before discharge he starts secondary prevention, is referred to cardiac rehabilitation, and receives stop-smoking support and diabetes review.

debrief: The ECG, not troponin, triggers the STEMI pathway.
NICE NG185: primary PCI if within 12 hours and deliverable within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could be given; otherwise fibrinolysis.
Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) usually means right coronary artery occlusion; look for right ventricular involvement and heart block.
Secondary prevention and rehabilitation start before discharge.

cases.title: Vomiting and drowsy with type 1 diabetes

steps.text: Jack, 19, has type 1 diabetes. He stopped his insulin 2 days ago when he ran out, and now has vomiting, abdominal pain and deep sighing breathing at 30/min. He is drowsy but responsive.

ask.q: Which bedside tests should be done first?
options: Capillary glucose and blood ketones, then a venous blood gas
ask.why: Missed insulin, vomiting and Kussmaul breathing suggest DKA, which is diagnosed by glucose (or known diabetes), ketones above 3.0 mmol/L and acidosis (bicarbonate below 15 and/or venous pH below 7.3). A venous gas gives pH, bicarbonate and potassium quickly.

steps.text: Glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 5.1 mmol/L, venous pH 7.12, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 131 mmol/L.

options: IV fluids and a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion, continuing his basal insulin; no potassium in the first fluids while it is above 5.5 mmol/L, then frequent checks
Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin and oral fluids
Insulin infusion only until glucose is normal
ask.why: JBDS DKA management: IV fluids, a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion and continued basal insulin. Potassium is held while above 5.5 mmol/L but will fall with insulin, so it is checked frequently. Bicarbonate is not routine, and the infusion continues until ketones and acidosis resolve, not just until glucose normalises.

steps.text: Six hours later his glucose is 12 mmol/L but ketones are 2.6 mmol/L and pH 7.24. Potassium is now 3.9 mmol/L.

options: Switch to subcutaneous insulin and discharge
Add IV glucose and continue the insulin infusion, with potassium in the fluids
ask.why: When glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, glucose is added so insulin can continue to clear ketones. Potassium (now 3.9 and falling) is added to fluids. DKA resolves when ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L and pH above 7.3.

steps.text: Outcome: by the next morning ketones are 0.4 mmol/L and pH 7.36. He eats, restarts subcutaneous insulin and the diabetes specialist team reviews sick-day rules and how he can avoid running out of insulin.

debrief: DKA needs ketones above 3.0, glucose above 11 or known diabetes, and bicarbonate below 15 and/or pH below 7.3 (JBDS 2023).
Continue basal insulin; add glucose when it falls below 14 mmol/L so the infusion can clear ketones.
Serum potassium falls with insulin despite a normal or high starting value.
Resolution is ketones below 0.6 and pH above 7.3; address the precipitant before discharge.

cases.title: Confused and hypotensive after surgery

steps.text: Mrs Clarke, 67, is two days after an anterior resection for rectal cancer. The nurse calls because she is newly confused. RR 28, SpO₂ 91% on air, BP 84/46, HR 126, temperature 38.9 °C.

ask.q: What is her NEWS2 score and the appropriate response?
options: 15: emergency response including staff with critical care skills
ask.why: RR 3 + SpO₂ 3 + air 0 + systolic 3 + pulse 2 + new confusion 3 + temperature 1 = 15. A score of 7 or more needs an urgent or emergency response including critical care skills.

steps.text: You assess her using ABCDE. Her airway is patent. She is tachypnoeic with reduced air entry at the bases. Her peripheries are cool and mottled. Lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. Her abdomen is distended and tender with guarding.

ask.q: Which set of actions should happen within the first hour?
options: Oxygen to target, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluid bolus with reassessment, urine output monitoring and urgent senior surgical and critical care review
Oral antibiotics and review on the morning round
CT first, then decide on antibiotics
IV fluids only, since antibiotics can wait for culture results
ask.why: With suspected infection and NEWS2 of 7 or more, NICE NG253 calls for urgent senior assessment and antibiotics within 1 hour, plus lactate, cultures and fluids. Imaging should not delay antibiotics. A lactate above 2 mmol/L confirms high risk.

steps.text: Despite fluid resuscitation her mean arterial pressure stays at 58 mmHg and lactate is 3.8 mmol/L.

ask.q: How is her condition now best described?
ask.why: Sepsis-3 defines septic shock as sepsis needing vasopressors to maintain MAP at 65 mmHg or more with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids. She needs critical care for vasopressors.

steps.text: Outcome: CT shows a leak at the anastomosis. She returns to theatre for source control and is managed on intensive care with vasopressors and antibiotics, and recovers.

debrief: Calculate NEWS2 accurately; 7 or more needs an emergency response with critical care skills.
NICE NG253: suspected infection with NEWS2 of 7 or more means antibiotics within 1 hour and senior review.
Septic shock (Sepsis-3): vasopressors needed for MAP of 65 or more and lactate above 2 despite fluids.
Source control (here, the anastomotic leak) matters as much as antibiotics.

osce.title: Taking and presenting a focused history
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself with name and role, confirm the patient's name and date of birth, and gain consent
Open with an open question and let the patient speak; listen without interrupting early
Explore the presenting complaint (SOCRATES for pain), then focused closed questions for discriminating features and red flags
Ask about the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations
Past medical and surgical history, including previous similar episodes
Drug history including over-the-counter medicines, and allergies with the nature of each reaction
Family history relevant to the complaint
Social history: occupation, home and function, smoking in pack-years, alcohol in units, driving
Brief systems review for relevant positives and red flags
Summarise back to the patient to check understanding, explain the next steps, and invite questions
Thank the patient, then present: one-line opening, key positives and discriminating negatives, impression with differentials, and a plan
tips: Signpost transitions ('I'd now like to ask about your medicines').
Present only the negatives that change the likelihood of your differentials.
Follow your own medical school's mark scheme where its order differs.

osce.title: Respiratory examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm identity, explain the examination, gain consent and offer a chaperone
Position the patient at about 45° with the chest exposed appropriately
General inspection: breathlessness, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, cough or sputum, and clues such as inhalers, oxygen or a sputum pot
Hands: clubbing, peripheral cyanosis, nicotine staining, tremor or flap (CO₂ retention); radial pulse and respiratory rate
Face and neck: central cyanosis, conjunctival pallor, JVP, trachea position, cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes
Chest inspection for scars, deformity and symmetry of expansion
Palpation: chest expansion front and back; apex beat position
Percussion over equivalent areas on both sides, front and back, including the axillae
Auscultation of breath sounds and added sounds; vocal resonance where indicated
Check for sacral and ankle oedema
Thank the patient, help them redress, clean your hands and summarise, suggesting further tests (observations including SpO₂, peak flow, chest X-ray, ABG if indicated)
tips: Compare side to side at every stage.
Dullness with reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance suggests effusion; dullness with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance suggests consolidation.
COPD does not cause clubbing: if you find it, look for another cause.

osce.title: Cardiovascular examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm identity, explain the examination and gain consent; offer a chaperone
Position at about 45° with the chest exposed appropriately
General inspection: breathlessness, colour, scars, and nearby clues such as GTN spray or oxygen
Hands: temperature, clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, capillary refill; radial pulse rate and rhythm, comparing both sides
Blood pressure (measure or state that you would)
Face: conjunctival pallor, xanthelasma, central cyanosis, dental hygiene
Neck: JVP at 45°, then carotid pulse character one side at a time
Chest inspection, then palpate the apex beat and feel for heaves and thrills
Auscultate the mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary and aortic areas, timing with the carotid pulse, with positional manoeuvres
Lung bases for crackles; sacrum and ankles for oedema
Thank the patient, clean your hands and summarise, suggesting a 12-lead ECG and further tests
tips: An irregularly irregular pulse suggests AF: confirm with a 12-lead ECG.
Raised JVP, basal crackles and oedema suggest fluid overload (e.g. heart failure).

interpret.title: Lying and standing blood pressure
interpret.q: A 79-year-old on three antihypertensives reports dizziness on getting up. Using the NICE NG136 definition, how should these readings be interpreted?
options: No postural drop, because diastolic fell by less than 10 mmHg
Cannot be interpreted without a 10-minute reading
Postural hypotension: systolic fell by 24 mmHg at 1 minute
interpret.why: NICE NG136 defines postural hypotension as a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more (or diastolic of 10 mmHg or more) on standing. 138 − 114 = 24 mmHg at 1 minute, so the systolic criterion is met even though the diastolic fell by only 6 mmHg. A small pulse rise suggests the reflex response is blunted; a medication review is the natural next step.
optWhy: Either criterion is enough; the systolic fall of 24 mmHg meets it.
Readings at 1 and 3 minutes are sufficient for this definition.
The pulse rose by only 6 beats/min, nowhere near a postural tachycardia pattern.
Correct: 138 − 114 = 24 mmHg, above the 20 mmHg threshold.

interpret.title: Chest pain with ST elevation
interpret.q: A 61-year-old has 90 minutes of central chest pain and sweating. The lead II strip shows sinus rhythm at about 88/min with about 2.5 mm of ST elevation. The 12-lead ECG shows similar ST elevation in III and aVF, with ST depression in I and aVL. What is the best interpretation?
options: Anterior STEMI from left anterior descending occlusion
Inferior STEMI, most likely right coronary artery, with reciprocal lateral depression
interpret.why: ST elevation in II, III and aVF localises to the inferior wall, usually supplied by the right coronary artery, and reciprocal depression in I and aVL supports a true infarct. With symptom onset 90 minutes ago he should go straight to primary PCI under NICE NG185 if it can be delivered in time; troponin should not delay reperfusion.
optWhy: Anterior STEMI shows elevation in V1–V4, not the inferior leads.
Pericarditis causes widespread concave elevation without reciprocal depression (apart from aVR and V1).
Correct: inferior leads elevated, reciprocal change in I and aVL.
NSTEMI by definition lacks persistent ST elevation.
Early repolarisation does not cause reciprocal depression or this clinical picture.

interpret.title: Irregular pulse in a 72-year-old
interpret.q: A 72-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has palpitations. The strip shows no P waves and irregularly irregular narrow complexes, 19 in 10 seconds. What is the rhythm, ventricular rate and her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score?
interpret.why: Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm is AF. For an irregular rhythm, count complexes in 10 seconds and multiply by 6: 19 × 6 = 114/min. CHA₂DS₂-VASc: age 65–74 (1) + female (1) + hypertension (1) + diabetes (1) = 4, so anticoagulation is indicated under NICE NG196.
optWhy: Flutter has regular sawtooth waves and usually a regular ventricular rate; the score is also undercounted.
Correct: AF, 19 × 6 = 114/min, score 4.
190/min multiplies by 10 rather than 6, and the score omits one item.
Sinus arrhythmia has a P wave before each QRS and varies with breathing.

interpret.q: A 70-year-old with known COPD arrived by ambulance on high-concentration oxygen and is increasingly drowsy. (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) What is the best interpretation and immediate action?

Acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis with oxygen-associated hypercapnia: reduce oxygen to target 88–92% and assess for NIV
interpret.why: pH is low with a high PaCO₂, so this is a respiratory acidosis; the raised bicarbonate shows chronic renal compensation, so it is acute-on-chronic. Saturations of 98% on 35% oxygen are above the BTS target of 88–92% for people at risk of hypercapnic failure. Check: 9.0 kPa × 7.5 = 67.5 mmHg; 6.1 + log₁₀(30 ÷ (0.0307 × 67.5)) = 6.1 + log₁₀(14.5) ≈ 7.26. Titrate oxygen down to target and, if acidosis persists despite optimal treatment, start NIV.
optWhy: Bicarbonate is raised, not low; the acidosis is respiratory.
pH is low, so this is not an alkalosis.
A pH of 7.26 is acidaemic and needs action.
PaO₂ is not low on oxygen and PaCO₂ is raised; more oxygen would worsen hypercapnia.
Correct: raised PaCO₂ with acidaemia and compensatory bicarbonate, with excess oxygen.

interpret.title: Pleuritic pain after surgery
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 34-year-old has pleuritic chest pain 10 days after knee surgery; the sample was taken on air. (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) Which interpretation fits best?

interpret.why: PaO₂ is below 8 kPa with a low PaCO₂: type 1 respiratory failure. A high pH with low PaCO₂ and normal bicarbonate is an acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation. Check: 4.0 × 7.5 = 30 mmHg; 6.1 + log₁₀(22 ÷ (0.0307 × 30)) = 6.1 + log₁₀(23.9) ≈ 7.48. With this history PE is likely; the two-level Wells score guides CTPA.

Correct: hypoxaemia with low PaCO₂ and alkalaemia.
Bicarbonate is normal, so the alkalosis is respiratory, not metabolic.
PaO₂ of 7.6 kPa on air is clearly abnormal.

interpret.title: Jaundice and itching

interpret.q: A 66-year-old has painless jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and itching. (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) What pattern do the liver tests show and what is the most appropriate first imaging?
options: Cholestatic pattern; abdominal ultrasound to look for biliary dilatation
Normal synthetic function excludes significant disease

Painless jaundice with pale stools and dark urine in an older adult raises concern about obstruction from malignancy such as pancreatic cancer, so ultrasound to look for biliary dilatation is the first step.
optWhy: Correct: ALP/GGT-dominant cholestasis; ultrasound first.
Transaminases are only modestly raised compared with ALP and GGT.
Gilbert's causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal enzymes and normal urine colour.
Normal albumin does not exclude obstruction or malignancy.

interpret.title: Lumbar puncture 14 hours after a thunderclap headache
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: CT head 10 hours after a sudden severe headache was normal. (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) How should this CSF be interpreted?
interpret.why: Bilirubin on spectrophotometry (xanthochromia) at least 12 hours after onset indicates blood that has been in the CSF long enough for red cells to break down, which supports subarachnoid haemorrhage (NICE NG228). Red cells that stay high from the first to the third tube also fit, whereas a traumatic tap usually shows clearing.
optWhy: A traumatic tap usually shows falling red cells across tubes and no bilirubin.
GBS gives raised protein without red cells or xanthochromia.
Bacterial meningitis gives a high neutrophil count and low glucose; white cells are near normal here.
Correct: xanthochromia 14 hours after onset indicates SAH.
Red cells, bilirubin and raised protein are abnormal.

interpret.title: Vomiting young adult with type 1 diabetes
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has missed insulin for 2 days. (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) What is the anion gap, and which statement about potassium management is correct?
options: Anion gap 26; do not add potassium to the first fluids, recheck often because insulin will lower it
Anion gap 26; give potassium immediately because total-body potassium is low
Anion gap 8; this is a normal anion gap acidosis
Anion gap 34; start oral potassium binders
interpret.why: Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 131 − (97 + 8) = 26 mmol/L, raised, from ketoacids. JBDS advises not adding potassium while it is above 5.5 mmol/L, but total-body potassium is depleted and insulin drives potassium into cells, so it must be rechecked frequently and replaced once 5.5 or below with urine output.
optWhy: Correct: gap 26; hold potassium while above 5.5 and monitor closely.
Potassium is not added while above 5.5 mmol/L, despite total-body depletion.
8 is the bicarbonate, not the gap; the gap is raised.
34 adds potassium to the cations; binders would be dangerous as potassium will fall with insulin.

interpret.title: Potassium 7.0 mmol/L
interpret.q: A 70-year-old with AKI has potassium 7.0 mmol/L on a non-haemolysed sample. The lead II strip shows a rate of 58/min, tall peaked T waves and QRS 3.5 small squares wide. What does the strip show and what is the first treatment?
options: Normal ECG; give a potassium binder
Hyperkalaemic changes with a broad QRS (0.14 s); give IV calcium first
interpret.why: 3.5 small squares × 0.04 s = 0.14 s, a broad QRS; with peaked T waves and bradycardia this is a dangerous hyperkalaemic ECG. UKKA guidance: protect the heart with IV calcium, then shift potassium with insulin–glucose and remove it.
optWhy: Peaked T waves and a broad QRS are clearly abnormal and need immediate cardiac protection.
PR of 0.20 s is at the upper limit and is not the key abnormality; atropine does not treat hyperkalaemia.
Correct: broad QRS and peaked T waves; IV calcium first.
The rhythm is slow and sinus, not a tachycardia.

interpret.q: An 82-year-old on ramipril, furosemide, spironolactone and ibuprofen has had 4 days of diarrhoea. (Reference ranges are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.) What is the KDIGO stage and the potassium severity band?

A 2.5-fold rise over days is clearly AKI.

12 misses one 3-point parameter.
